speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have just
suggested, and, the hon. leader of the opposition has agreed, that it might be preferable to print the declaration in Hansard; then it will be available to all hon. members.

There are others besides members of the house who would like to get a copy.
The declaration follows:
Permanent Court Of International Justice Declaration made by the Hon. Raoul Dandurand, before signing the optional clause on behalf of His Majesty's government in Canada
Geneva, September 20, 1929.
On behalf of His Majesty's government in Canada and subject to ratification, I accept as compulsory "ipso facto" and without special convention, on condition of reciprocity, the jurisdiction of the court in conformity with article 36, paragraph 2, of the statute, for a period of ten years and thereafter until such time as notice may be given to terminate the acceptance, over all disputes arising after ratification of the present declaration with regard to situations or facts subsequent to said ratification, other than:
disputes in regard to which parties have agreed or shall agree to have recourse to some other method of peaceful settlement, and
disputes with the government of any other member of the league which is a member of the British commonwealth of nations, all of which disputes shall be settled in such manner as the parties have agreed or shall agree, and disputes with regard to questions which by international law fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada,
and subject to the condition that His Majesty's government in Canada reserve the right to require that proceedings in the court 2419-69
shall be suspended in respect of any dispute which has been submitted to and is under consideration by the Council of the League of Nations, provided that notice to suspend is given after the dispute has been submitted to the council and is given within ten days of the notification of the initiation of the proceedings in the court, and provided also that such suspension shall be limited to a period of twelve months or such longer period as may be agreed by the parties to the dispute or determined by a decision of all the members of the council other than the parties to the dispute.
R. Dandurand. NATURAL RESOURCES

speechtext: What progress has been made and what action has been taken to ensure to civil servants in Canada, and all employees of the Dominion government, the eight-hour day?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
With respect to this question, Mr. Speaker, I assume that the hon. member (Mr. Adshead) has in mind two sets of employees, those in the government service and those engaged on government contracts. I may say that an order in council which was passed a few days ago gives the eight-hour day to the direct employees of the Dominion government. I am glad to table a minute of the privy council, and the order.
The documents follow:

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Certified to be a true copy of a minute of a
meeting of the committee of the Privy 
Council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on the 27th March, 1930.
The committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 19th March, 1930, from the Minister of Labour, submitting as follows:
1.	That is was recognized in the labour part of the Treaty of Versailles and the corresponding provisions of the other treaties of peace, that the well-being-physical, moral and intellectual-of industrial wage earners is of supreme international importance, and that although differences of climate, habits and customs, economic principles and industrial traditions, make strict uniformity in the conditions of labour difficult of immediate attainment, there are methods and principles for regulating labour conditions which all industrial communities should endeavour to apply, so far as their special circumstances will permit.
2.	That approval was expressed in the peace treaties of the principle of the eight-hour working day.
3.	- That a draft convention was adopted at the first session of the conference of the international labour organization (League of Nations) in 1919 to limit hours of work in industrial undertakings to eight hours per day.
4.	That the draft convention above mentioned was referred in 1924 to the select standing committee on industrial and international relations of the House of Commons of Canada for examination and report.
5.	That on the recommendation of the committee on industrial and international relations of the House of Commons, approved by the House of Commons, the draft convention on hours of work in industrial undertakings was referred by Order in Council to the Supreme Court of Canada with a view to determining the jurisdiction of the federal and provincial authorities, respectively, on this subject.
6.	That the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada contained the following declaration: "The subject matter is generally within the competence of the legislatures of the provinces but the authority vested in these legislatures does not enable them to give the force of law to provisions such as those contained in the draft convention in relation to servants of the Dominion Government, or to legislate for those parts of Canada which are not within the boundaries of a province."
7.	That a report from the Civil Service Commission, which was submitted to your Excellency in Council under date of February 16, 1925, showed that the standard daily hours of work of monthly rate employees in the government departments are from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with an interval for luncheon and a half-holi-

Questions
day on Saturday, and that the standard hours of prevailing rate employees, numbering 1,576 in Ottawa and 18,264 outside Ottawa (of whom 12,247 were postmasters paid on percentage basis), are 44 hours per week, based on an eight-hour day for five days, and 4 hours, or a half-day, on Saturday. Certain exceptions to these standard hours of work were also noted in the report of the Civil Service Commission.
8.	That request has been made to the government for the granting of the eight-hour day to its own employees.
9.	That it is desirable that the principle of the eight-hour day should be applied to any branches of the public service of Canada in which it is not now observed.
The minister accordingly recommends that, except in cases where the work of employees is intermittent in character, or the application of this rule is not deemed to be practicable or in the public interest, the hours of work of any employees of the Dominion government who are still required to work more than eight hours daily be reduced to eight hours daily, with a half-holiday on Saturday.
The committee concur in the forgegoing recommendation and submit the same for approval.
E. J. Lemaire.

2.	Mr. Harrison is fair wages officer and mediator of the Department of Labour with headquarters at Vancouver, B.C., and his territory comprises the four western provinces. The payment under this vote is to cover his travelling expenses while engaged in gathering information as to prevailing wage rates in western Canada, which information is used in connection with the preparation of schedules containing labour conditions-wages and hours -for insertion in specifications and contracts governing federal government construction work. This officer is required to visit the
various federal government undertakings in his territory during the period of construction and ascertain definitely that the wage schedule applicable to the particular work is posted in a conspicuous place on the work and is easily accessible to the workmen employed thereon; also to ascertain by investigation that these labour conditions are being fully complied with. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
1 and 2. The sovereign right of all nations to the use of every radio channel is recognized, thus Canada has always enjoyed the right to
allot any of the frequencies in the broadcast band to any radio broadcasting stations under its jurisdiction.
It is nevertheless recognized that until technical development progresses to the stage where radio interference can be eliminated, special arrangements between neighbouring countries are desirable in order to minimize such interference.
To this end, negotiations were entered into with the United States, immediately on the passing of the United States radio act in February, 1927, with a view to concluding a formal agreement for a division of the 96 available broadcast channels between Canada and that country.
The division demanded by the United States representatives, based primarily on the relative populations of the two countries, was not acceptable to the Canadian representatives, and the conference was therefore adjourned.
In December, 1928, Canada notified all nations subscribing to the Internationa] Radio Convention, through the medium of the International Radiotelegraph Bureau, Berne, as follows:-
"The question of the division of frequencies in the broadcast band between the broadcasting stations in the North America area has been the subject of negotiations between the interested countries, but, so far, no agreement has been reached. The International Radiotelegraph Convention of Washington, 1927, becomes effective on January 1, 1929, and in submitting Canada's list of broadcasting stations for publication in the official list, in accordance with the provisions of the convention, the Canadian administration has refrained from notifying the temporary and inadequate assignment on which its broadcasting stations are now operating and desires it to be understood that pending the consummation of an agreement between the administrations in the North America area in regard to broadcasting, the Canadian administration in no way waives the right it considers it enjoys under the International Radio Convention in regard to the use of a reasonable proportion of the broadcast frequencies available in the above mentioned area."
'Mr. Heenan.]

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in connection with the printing of the proceedings which have taken place before the committee on returned soldiers' problems, I find that 950 copies of the reports issued from day to day have been absorbed by the Canadian Legion, leaving a very small number for circulation among the members. As a matter of fact, some of the members have not been able to secure a copy at all. Of course it is desirable that the legion should circulate these reports as freely as possible, but in view of the fact that they represent only about 75,000 of the entire membership of the overseas forces, I think it will be agreed that something should be done to make it possible to circulate larger numbers of these reports. I am bound to say that the distribution office could give us no reasonable explanation as to why the members of parliament were not furnished with these reports, while 950 copies were absorbed by the legion, under someone's orders. Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister, for Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 22, to amend the Indian Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Eskimo affairs.

Will the hon. minister
explain the object of this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Some years ago it was thought wise to place the Eskimos under the control of the Indian department but it has been found that this does not work out very acceptably as we have no Indian officers in the territory where the Eskimos are located. The officers of the Department of the Interior are located there and we are asking that the control of the Eskimos be placed under the Northwest Territories council and the Department of the Interior rather than under the Indian department.

Was the control under the
Northwest territories council?
Indian Act Amendment

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Up until
three years ago.
What difficulty has been experienced in the interval?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Royal Northwest Mounted Police are now located along Coronation gulf up in Baffin Land, in the territories frequented by the Eskimos, and they seem to offer at the present time the best agency to look after the Eskimos, and in addition to that the officers of the Department of the Interior are in that territory. I think it would work out much more acceptably to allow those officers and the mounted police to supervise whatever control is necessary over these people.
What is the Eskimo population?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We know that we have over four thousand Eskimos, although we are not sure about the number.
Has any census been taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Figures as to population have been obtained through our officers in the Northwest Territories, as well as the mounted police.
Are these people considered to be British subjects in all respects?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Apparently that is a ruling I am not competent to give.
A ruling made by whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They are assumed to be British subjects. As my hon. friend knows, we have taken over the control of the territory, which control has not been disputed in any particular except with respect to one small portion. The Danish government have presented a claim based upon the explorations made by Otto Sverdrup, and at the present time we are endeavouring to settle that claim.
What is the origin of these people, were they originally Indian?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Eskimo.
Or are they Mongolians; of what race are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend has asked me a question which I cannot answer.
A good deal would depend upon that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There is a difference of opinion. Many hold that they are Mongolian but I do not think anyone can prove it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Some people say they are Scotch.
They are treated as wards of the government and not as full-fledged citizens; that is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

I understand that the government hitherto has treated them as being originally an Indian tribe and for some time past has assumed the guardianship of these people in the same manner as it assumes guardianship over the Indians. Are these people entitled to the franchise where the Indian is not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Well, our position with respect to the Eskimos and the territory over which they roam is that we claim that we own the territory, and therefore the residents in that territory must be Canadian. No treaties have been arranged with the Eskimos as with the Indians in other parts of Canada. These people are a nomadic race and are found in widely scattered territories. As my hon. friend knows, the Indians locate in some particular spot, but that is not true of the Eskimos. They return annually to their old camping grounds but so far we have not treated the Eskimos as we have the original Indians of Canada.
To what territory is the hon. minister referring?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Coronation gulf, Melville island, Baffin Land and all the territory north.
How many Eskimos are in that territory?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have
answered that; we know there are about four thousand.
The minister did not answer my question; if the Eskimo were seeking a franchise in this country, would he be entitled to vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I imagine that he would be a citizen of the country unless the same process had been gone through as with the Indians; which has not been done up to the present time.
That has not been done up to date?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No.

Indian Act Amendment
They will continue to be wards of the government or of the Northwest Territories council as formerly?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I doubt if they would be considered wards of the government in the sense that the Indian is a ward. They are granted educational facilities, provided largely by the missionaries, the same as the Indians, and in times of necessity they are given relief. Outside of that, no treaty has been enacted which would designate them as aborigines of that territory.
There are Indians in Canada with whom we have not negotiated a treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Very few.
But there are some?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
The Eskimo would be in exactly the same position.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: My hon. friend would be correct in that.
If one had the franchise then the other would have it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Is my hon. friend concerned about the franchise?
I just added that clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Indian has not the right to the franchise until he is enfranchised.
The minister argues that the Eskimo would have the franchise because he has not entered into a treaty with the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is a very fine legal argument and one which I am not competent to answer.

Do I understand the
minister to say that Eskimos who are British subjects and wards of the government, exercise the franchise or have the right of exercising it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: So far as I am aware, there has never been an election, in which they could exercise the franchise.
Will they exercise it under the proposed enlargement of the Yukon territory as an electoral unit?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have never heard the question raised before. I noticed in the press a few w'eeks ago, someone raised it, but I would much prefer to take the position suggested by my hon. friend that not all of these Eskimos, but some of them, have been subject to the bounty of the Canadian government and in every respect are treated as wards of the government, although one cannot, I think, legally say that they are wards. That is the point.
Would the minister consider them as wards of the government, entitled to the franchise?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I would not care to give my hon. friend an answer offhand on that point. I will make inquiry and be prepared to give an answer later, but I am not going to assume the responsibility of saying that the Eskimos would be enfranchised.

I should like to call the minister's attention to this question which I asked on the tenth of March:
Are adult Eskimos, being British subjects, residents of Canada for the period required by Dominion Elections Act, qualified to vote at elections of a member of the House of Commons?
The minister's reply was:
Yes, Eskimos who are British subjects by birth or naturalization.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They would be identical with an enfranchised Indian in that respect. That is the position of an Indian when he is granted enfranchisement and foregoes the benefit of his tribal membership.
Would an Eskimo, in order to exercise the right of voting, have to be enfranchised the same as an Indian?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am not
clear as to the status of an Eskimo. My difficulty is this: the Eskimo is there; to all intents and purposes he is a ward of the government so far as care in time of necessity is concerned, but I believe there is no treaty existing nor would I say that his status has been defined. If, however, he were enfranchised under his own name he would be in the same category as an Indian who had been enfranchised in exactly the same way.
Do I understand the minister to say that this answer given by him on the tenth of this month is not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think it is correct.

How does an Indian become enfranchised?
Indian Act Amendment

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: By consent of the band to which he belongs, by foregoing all the rights he holds as a member of the tribe .and becoming a citizen of the country, and by order in council.
Might I ask the minister whether the government considers, as a matter of principle, that Eskimos, who are wards of or who receive bounty from the government, could exercise the franchise?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I did not say that they were wards. I want my hon. friend to get my explanation correctly. What I say is that the Eskimos have in the past been in receipt of bounty from the Canadian government.

I included that in my
question.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: What status that might or might not give them, I am not prepared to say. It is a strictly legal question, but I say that the Eskimos have not, to my knowledge, made any treaty with the Canadian government.

I was asking not as a
legal question but as a matter of principle or policy whether the minister considers that Eskimos who are receiving bounty or any kind of favour from the Canadian government, should exercise the franchise?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I shall have to leave that question to be answered by the Department of Justice. I cannot give a legal opinion on it.

As I understand the matter, Canada claims sovereignty roughly from the forty-ninth parallel to the northern portion of the continent, and any British subject resident within Canada, if he is in an electoral district, is entitled to vote. Is an Eskimo born within this area over which Canada claims sovereignty, a British subject?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Eskimos who are British subjects have certainly the right to vote, just as any other British subject. They are not Indians. In the Dominion Elections Act under qualifications of electors, there is an exception for Indians ordinarily resident on an Indian reservation. The Eskimos are not in that category. Moreover, they are not Indians. There is nothing to disqualify an Eskimo simply because he is an Eskimo. That is my first impression.
I would understand my hon. friend is speaking as Minister of Justice when he gives the opinion and would be prepared to stand by it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is not altogether fair.
Quite fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He asks me what is my impression at the moment. I cannot give more than that. I have never given any consideration to the matter, but there is no doubt in my mind, speaking at the moment, that an Eskimo is not disqualified simply because he happens to be an Eskimo.

To follow the question a
little further, may I ask this:	If the bill
which affects the constituency of the Yukon passes the house and the Northwest Territories are incorporated with the Yukon as an electoral district, will these nomadic tribes who are receiving bounty occasionally from the government, be entitled to vote whether or not they have a permanent place of residence? It is a fact that they are objects of charity from time to time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They will be entitled to vote if they do not fall under any of the exceptions which disqualify people from voting.
Is there any exception which would disqualify them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend is free
to consult the Dominion Elections Act just as I am.
The Minister of Justice being so ready with his opinion as to the rights of British subjects, I thought he would be equally ready with information concerning the Dominion Elections Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see
under the rules that an hon. member is not entitled to ask legal advice of the Minister of Justice. That is not my function.

The question is of vital
interest to the house and I think it should be answered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps I can have a
private talk with my hon. friend and give him all the enlightenment he desires.

I do not wish to
fee too persistent in regard to this matter, but the Minister of the Interior has gone officially on record as giving his opinion that Eskimos have the right to vote. They are qualified under the Dominion Elections Act. Do I take it that the Minister of Justice agrees with that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
When my
hon. friend says he is quoting me, I presume he is quoting an answer to a question?

Indian Act Amendment
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is a
definite statement that Eskimos who are British subjects are entitled to vote.

The question is:
Are adult Eskimos, being British subjects, residents of Canada for the period required by the Dominion Elections Act, qualified to vote at elections of a member of the House of Commons?
The minister replied:
Yes, Eskimos who are British subjects by birth or naturalization.
The question did not apply to United States or other foreign Eskimos; it was only Canadian Eskimos I was referring to.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon.
friend asked a very distinct question:	Are
Eskimos who are enfranchised entitled to vote? Certainly they are. Indians who are enfranchised are entitled to vote. That is the question he asked.

I said Eskimos
with the qualifications of other electors under the Dominion Elections Act. Then the government say that they are entitled to vote.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Unless they are excluded
under the act, how can they be prevented from voting?
Surely the Solicitor General with his fund of legal knowledge knows why they should be excluded.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The Dominion Elections
Act recites very plainly who are electors and who are not, and unless a certain class of people are excluded under the act, they have a right to vote.

May I ask the Solicitor
General if the mere receipt of charity from the Dominion government is a bar to voting?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is wrong about that.
I do not say that it is. In my opinion it is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I read the section of the Dominion Elections Act which relates to persons supported by charity? Under section 30 persons are disqualified.
Who, at the time of an election, are prisoners undergoing punishment for criminal offences, or are patients in lunatic asylums, or are maintained in whole or in part as inmates receiving public charitable support or care in municipal poor houses or houses of industry, or are inmates receiving public charitable support, other than for war services, in any institution receiving aid from the government of a province under any statute in that behalf

for the whole period of such election.
Surely the Eskimos do not come in that class.
So they would be entitled to the franchise?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think so.
That is exactly what I said, and I was trying to find out if the Minister of Justice agreed with me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What is it the hon.
member is objecting to?
To their receiving the franchise and then receiving support from this government.
The classes just read by the minister would not include the ordinary Indian.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Indians come under another exception.
Does the Minister of Justice consider it sound in principle that a person who is in receipt of a bounty administered by officials of the government should be entitled to the franchise?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no opinion to offer as to that, except to say that it is the law.
Does the minister think it ought to be the law? It opens itself to the most vicious sort of abuses?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not in favour of restrictions as to the franchise, if my hon. friend wants to know.
Nor am I.
What would the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg say about the unemployed who are getting assistance from the government right along having the franchise? Would he exclude them?
I do not know any that are getting assistance from this government.

It would not make any difference whether it was a Tory government or a Liberal government. If my hon. friend applied his principle to the unemployed who are receiving assistance from the government, a lot of Nova Scotia people would be disfranchised.
Many of them are, for municipal purposes.

While this discussion is very interesting, I would remind the minister of my question regarding the position of Indians who are at present not under treaty.
Indian Act Amendment

A reading of the clause of the Dominion Elections Act just quoted by the Minister of Justice would indicate that any Indian who did not ordinarily reside on a reserve had the right of franchise.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Oh no.

Any Indian not ordinarily resident upon a reserve is excepted from the disabilities applying to the Indian upon the reserve. I think I aan correct in that, and certainly the Indians who are not under treaty would very largely out-number the Eskimos of Canada. So all these arguments would apply equally to men living in the northern parts of this Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is wrong, if he will permit me. The Indians have not the franchise unless they are enfranchised.

And if they do not receive
a bounty.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
They may.
They would not receive payments under the Indian Act.
That is what I mean.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
They are
Canadian citizens with all the privileges of citizenship. But no Indian is entitled to the franchise until he is enfranchised. An Indian is debarred from the privileges of the franchise until he becomes an enfranchised Indian under the act.

There is no question about the ordinary Indian residing in Canada being a Canadian, and I say that a band of Indians who have no treaty with the government, and never had, should be placed in the same position at least as the Eskimo. There can be no reason why the Eskimo should be preferred while the Indian, who is, to say the least, just as intelligent, should be debarred from the franchise.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The Indian
Act provides as to the steps that are to be taken to enfranchise an Indian, and he is not enfranchised until those steps are taken. The question that arises about the Eskimo is a different one altogether. An Eskimo would have to be construed to be an Indian and subjected to all the restrictions of the Indian Act, which he is not.

If this act passes, the
Eskimo and the non-treaty Indian are in exactly the same position. There is absolutely no difference between them.
(Mr. Arthurs.]

I am glad to hear this discussion about the Eskimos. Now that the eyes of Canada are turning towards the north it is interesting to note that public interest is being taken in these people. Many hon. members of this house are no doubt aware that two or three years ago Pere Duchaussois, of the Oblate order, published a book, entitled "Aux Glaces Polaires," which has had a very extensive circulation all through Europe, and has been crowned by the French Academy. The book gives a most complete account of that northern country from the historical perspective, and especially of the Eskimo proper. The Oblate fathers, under Mgr. Turquetil, have been carrying on missionary work there for many years, and so also have the Anglicans. I am glad to know that the government is now going to take a larger interest in these farthest removed inhabitants of the north. The hardships with which they have to contend are almost inconceivable and, as described by Pere Duchaussois in his book, are indeed a revelation. Modern science to-day has brought the radio to the Eskimos, and through the good offices of the Royal North West Mounted Police day by day they are being brought into closer touch with civilization. One reason perhaps more than any other why they should receive sympathy and assistance of Canada is that they have to endure great hardships. I think we should extend to them the inestimable privilege of being recognized as British subjects, entitled to all the privileges that come to those who enjoy British citizenship.

I have been looking into this bill very carefully. The minister draws a sharp distinction between the Eskimo and the Indian. Will he be good enough to tell us how he decides whether a person is an Eskimo or an Indian? What are the grounds of distinction?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not
think one would have very much difficulty in deciding which was an Indian and which was an Eskimo by the appearance. That is one test. Another is language; to some extent, also, their habits. After all, there is not so very much difference between an Englishman and a Scotchman.
Oh, yes.

Everybody will
not agree with the minister there. What I really mean is this: There must be some description of an Indian and some description of an Eskimo. The minister says that a person could tell the difference between them by their appearance, but the minister himself is not going to decide which of these thousands of

Indian Act Amendment
people are Eskimos and which are Indians. He must lay down some rule or regulation by which the officials can decide whether a man is an Indian or an Eskimo. I take it that they are all children of the wild, nomadic tribes, living very differently from us, both the Indian and the Eskimo. I think the minister ought in specific words to draw the distinction between the two when the act makes such a difference between them.

I would point out to the minister that outside the first clause of this bill there is no word relating to Eskimos, nor are they referred to in any part of the text. Section 1 provides:
Subsection 2 of section 4 of the Indian Act, chapter 98 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, is repealed.
That is the clause which places the care of Eskimos under the Indian department. According to the minister's statement, the bill is to empower him to direct the affairs of the Eskimos, but, as I say, except for the first section of the bill there is no reference to Eskimos, the other sections deal exclusively with Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is referring to subsection 2 of section 4 of the Indian Act, which provides that the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs shall have charge of Eskimo affairs. There was never an37 provision made as to how that charge should be carried out, because we have not had the same contact with the Eskimo that we have had with the Indian. Prior to bringing the Eskimo under the control of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, our contact with him had been through the officials of the Northwest Territories branch. Even that was not a very drastic change, because the minister in charge of that branch is the Minister of the Interior. However, as to whether that had the effect of bringing the Eskimo entirely under the Indian Act, I am not prepared to say. As to the definition of an Eskimo there is no doubt that the racial distinction between even the most northern Indian and the Eskimo is very marked. I do not think anyone would have a great deal of difficulty in distinguishing one from the other.

But the minister himself would not be making the distinction. Ho must have the Eskimo defined so that those who are administering Indian affairs may distinguish between the Eskimo and the Indian. They are both native races. I do not see how the minister can draft a definition which will hold water in all cases.
Aside from the point that is being discussed at the moment, does the minister think the nomadic Eskimo has a sufficient knowledge of our institutions to cast an intelligent vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I was not
thinking about the question of voting prior to- the Eskimo being put in charge of the Indian department nor since; I was simply looking at as a matter of administration. If the Eskimo is conceded to have a vote, that is something I have given no attention to whatever. The question of enfranchising or disenfranchising the Eskimo never entered my mind. As I say,-it is simply a question of administration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I find it difficult to understand how the hon. minister can say that, if he looks at the explanation he has placed opposite section 1 of the bill. This is his explanatory note:
This repeal is due to the fact that by order of His Excellency the Governor General in Council, dated the 31st of August, 1927, and made in pursuance of the provisions of chapter. 6 8-9 George V. (1918) and the amendment thereto, chapter 23, 15-16 George Y. (1925) the charge of Eskimo affairs was transferred to the Commissioner of the Northwest territories, Department of the Interior.
So that at the moment it is in the hands of the Commissioner of the Northwest Territories?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, but it was for a short period under the control of the Department of Indian Affairs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But the point I am making is this: What authority did that give to repeal section 2 of the act? That act is in the revised statutes of 1927 which came into force in 1927. Subsection 2 of section 4 provides: The Superintendent General of Indian Affairs shall have charge of Eskimo affairs.
How' can an order in council passed antecedently to the date of these revised statutes repeal a provision of these statutes?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We could
not legally repeal it. We were doing it for administration purposes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is not correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend. We knew perfectly well that we had not power to override the statute, but as a matter of administration, to obviate the duplicating of officials, we have as a matter of fact been supervising Eskimo affairs by the North West Territories branch. We are simply asking the repeal of the section now.

Indian Act Amendment

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then what happens is this: The Minister of the Interior comes in to the House of Commons and says that under the authority of a statute passed in 1918 and of another passed in 1925, on the 31st August, 1927, which is over two years ago, he did an illegal thing and has been doing it ever since. Mr. LAPOINTE: In what way?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He says so; he says he knows it is illegal.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Whether he said so or not, he was wrong.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Was he? How could the governor in council in 1927 repeal the provisions of a statute that came into force as a part of the revised statutes of Canada a few months before under the authority of the statutes of 1918 and 1925?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is my hon. friend sure it was a few months before? My impression is that the revised statutes of 1927 came into force only in December of that year. That would be after this transfer.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The proclamation is the 22nd day of December, 1927. The order in council would have been passed in the summer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But the revised statutes of Canada are those of 1927.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I know; but the proclamation which put them into force is dated December, 1927.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Certainly; that is my
point. I he statute came into force subsequent to the order in council, and the statute governs. Therefore the order in council is illegal. That is what the minister admits. I have now the statute before me. It is chapter 98 and it came into force, as the Solicitor General says, after August, 1927. I thought it was September; he says December. Subsection 4 of section 2 of the Indian Act, being chapter 98 reads as follows:
The Minister of the Interior, or the head of any other department appointed for that purpose by the governor in council, shall be the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, and shall as such, have the control and management ot the lands and property of the Indians in Canada.
Of the lands and property of the Indians in Canada. Subsection 2 reads:
The Superintendent General of Indian Affairs shall have charge of Eskimo affairs.
That section was passed before 1924. Now the Solicitor General says this statute was in force in December, 1927.
TMr. C. A. Stewart. ]

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is the proclamation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the date?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Some time in December.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I thought so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It has no effect whatsoever on this.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It has all the effect in the world. How can the governor in council do something which the statute prohibits?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As soon as my hon.
friend gives me the floor, I will explain.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That is in February of
1928.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Even if it were before I do not think it would matter. As the explanatory note says, this transfer of powers took place under the statute of 1948, during the good days of a government other than the present one.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It says 192S, finally.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In 1918. In 1925 it
simply amended and made clearer the provisions of the statute of 1918.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In 1918 it was enacted that the governor in council shall have power to transfer any powers, duties or functions from one minister of the crown to another, and from one department to another, or to combine two departments under one minister, and so on. It was amended in 1925 to the effect that the duties and powers are to be exercised by the minister in the department to which the transfer of duties is made.
The 1925 statute simply states that when the powers conferred by the statutes of 1918 are exercised all the duties which were under the deputy minister or officers of the first department shall be exercised by the deputy minister and the officers of the second department. It is under those two statutes that in 1927 the Eskimo branch was transferred from the Department of Indian Affairs to the Department of the Interior. It was perfectly legal to do so, but I believe my hon. friend says it comes in conflict with the revised statutes of Canada. The Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) now hands me chapter 165 of the revised statutes of Canada, which reenact the statutes of 1918 and 1925.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At any time, whether before or after the proclamation putting into force the revised statutes of 1927, the gover-

Indian Act Amendment
nor in council has the authority to transfer one branch of a department to another department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And this has	been	done.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not see	the	occasion
for the discussion on section 1 of this bill, which merely enacts the law as it stands at the present time. The effect of section 1 is merely to make this law coincide with the existing situation; this is an anomaly which is being repealed by section 1 of the present act. It is a condition which no longer exists.
Has the minister before him the statutes of 1924? This particular clause we are dealing with was not passed in 1925, but in 1924.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it was 1925.

Subsection 2 of section 4 of the Indian Act provides:
The Superintendent General of Indian Affairs shall take charge of Eskimo affairs.
That is the same as chapter 47, section 1, revised statutes of Ganada, 1924.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
It is 1924, and not 1925.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is talking about another statute. This was changed by the governor in council in 1927, acting in accordance with or under the authority of the statutes of 1925. It can be done at any time and in any department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am sorry the minister
does not appreciate the point we are making. We fully agree with everything he has said, but he does not touch the point. The Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) sees it, however. The point is that the transfer of administration from one department to another is accomplished under the provisions of the statutes of 1918 and 1925, the substance of which we find in chapter 161 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927. Chapter 98, however, of the revised statutes of Canada deals with the Indians of the country; it is the Indian Act. Under the provisions of subsection 2, section 4, of that statute, it is positively enacted that the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs shall have charge of matters pertaining to Eskimos. That cannot be repealed, except by this parliament. The transfer of the administration to the Northwest Territories branch does not relieve the minister of his responsibility; on the contrary, he still has that responsibility. What we are endeavouring to 2419-70J
ascertain is why he is desirous of divesting himself of the authority which parliament placed upon him in 1924. That is the whole story. There is no variance between the Minister of Justice and ourselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is the result the
Minister of the Interior wishes to effect by the present section of the bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To make it coincide with the present situation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No. Let me illustrate it in this way. The Minister of Justice has under his control both the penitentiaries and the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. If he desired he could, by section 161 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, transfer the administration of the northwest mounted police to the Prime Minister, as was done, in fact, on one occasion. It is not competent, however, by order in council, to repeal this subsection of section 4 which affirmatively places the responsibility for the Eskimos in the hands of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. For what reason is this being done? It does not touch the administration, but it touches ministerial responsibilities, and as to who shall be the responsible minister in this house for the Eskimos. That subsection states that the Minister of the Interior or the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs is the responsible minister. Why must there be no responsible minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is one.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Who is to be the responsible minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Minister of the
Interior.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But he only gets it
under the section we are going to repeal. The transfer by the order in council for administration does not in any sense repeal the substantive section which places responsibility upon the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He is repealing it now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Who will be in charge of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He is.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am speaking about
ministerial responsibility in this house. It says that the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs is responsible for the affairs of the Eskimos, and that he is the only minister in this house who is responsible. Until some other minister is made responsible, he must be.
Indian Act Amendment

Why change it and thereby shift the responsibility, if all this is going to increase responsibility? That section was put in in 1924 to deal with a situation abqut which the minister must have knowledge. The Minister of the Interior knows that the condition of the Eskimos was very acute, there was starvation among them, and he must recall that situation. Some of the missionaries brought it to the attention of the minister. I, myself, recall going to the minister and calling it to his attention. That being the position, what minister is going to be responsible when this section is repealed?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The administration of the Northwest Territories is under the control of the Minister of the Interior, who at the moment happens to be also the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The statute says he shall be until someone else is appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If my hon. friend now is arguing that since in 1927 the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs was mentioned as the responsible minister, and that since now we are giving official control to the North West Territories branch the Minister of the Interior should be specifically mentioned, I have no objection.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister has grasped the point. Under our system of government there must be ministerial responsibility somewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then all my hon. friend desires is that in addition to this repeal there should be a section stating that the control is under the Minister of the Inerior?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I believe that should be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think there would be no objection to it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister sees the
point because, as the Solicitor General pointed out, the revised statutes did not come into force until February of 1928. That section now stands as the law, and of course the question of administration is very different from that of ministerial responsibility.
Now let us deal with the vital question involved, assuming that you repeal the statute. The Eskimos are nomads; they have no established communities in the sense in which the Indians were established when this country was discovered. Rightly or wrongly we think we have a better system than other countries have, because we have recognized the right of the aboriginal red man and his title, in
[Mr Bennett.]
part, to property in this country. When we made a treaty with the Indians we recognized them as distinct tribes; we enacted that they should have property rights in certain areas, and even yet we cannot part with those property rights without their consent, as the minister knows. For instance, if it is desirable for any purpose to secure 1,000 acres of land from a band of Indians, it requires a very great deal of effort and labour to bring about that result; they must be convened together in a certain way and they must have interpreters clearly to place before them what it is proposed to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon.
friend must remember that the act does give the superintendent general power in certain cases.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is so; there are provisions which vest an arbitrary power in the superintendent general, to a certain extent, but the whole theory of the act is that, as far as possible, the Indians should be treated as proprietors of their reserves.
Now we come to the Eskimos. They have no treaties with us; they have no established reserves, as the minister knows, and I think a few moments ago he used two words which describe the situation very well. He said they were nomadic tribes. How can we, having assumed it, divest ourselves of responsibility by endeavouring to treat them as settled persons in certain communities? At the moment the responsibility for providing the Eskimos with a living rests with us, and the minister recalls that at very great expense he sent an expedition to that northern country to provide them with food and medicine, if I remember correctly, when they were not really able to make a living for themselves. I think I can safely say that they are an uncivilized class of people; they hardly live in tribes and they have not developed any form of settled life.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They may be broken up a very great deal; one can scarcely say they are in tribes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I was coming to that. When we speak of them as a tribe we must remember that they have no settled communities in which they live, and I am told by those who have visited that country that during their summer they have no settled residences at all. They have no settlements, in the meaning of the term as it was used by the early pioneers with respect to the Indians. These people are not civilized as we use the word civilization. Whether or not the Indians are civilized is not the question. These

Indian Act Amendment
Eskimos are wards of this nation, and being wards the question of who assumes trusteeship for them becomes important.
At present the trustee is the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. That superintendent now proposes to divest himself of responsibility, saying that because the administration is vested with the Commissioner of the Northwest Territories it is going to be left with him, but that does not get away from the essential fact that the wardship continues. These people are wards of this nation, and when the other day I heard a discussion with regard to the Eskimo having a vote I knew that if my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior were not in this house, and if politics and such matters were forgotten, he would regard it as one of the hugest jokes he ever heard. These wards of the nation are scattered far and wide, over mount and stream and sea. They are here to-day and far away to-morrow, and I am sure the Minister of Justice must realize that such wards of the nation are not people who should be entrusted with the franchise, because they are not a part of our civilized country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Surely this question
should be discussed in connection with the Dominion Elections Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No doubt that is correct, but at the same time it arises here, because we are divesting ourselves of a wardship and we are not naming the responsible minister who will communicate to this house the conduct of his wardship. It is quite clear that the order in council transferring the administration of this matter to the Commissioner of the Northwest Territories covers the matter of administration, but it does not get away from the essential question of the responsibility for the wardship of these people.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I quite agree with my hon. friend. I do not care to discuss the question of the enfranchisement of the Eskimo; to be very frank, it never occurred to me that such a question would arise. There is no doubt that if distress arises among these people, to that extent they are wards of the Canadian government, and if we allowed famine or pestilence to run riot among them we would be called to account. They are not Indians as we know Indians, with chiefs and councils and all the paraphernalia which has been set up by the Indians for the management of their affairs. These people congregate in small family groups; no doubt they have leaders, but apparently in discussing matters of importance with our officials they all speak, each for himself.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They have no chiefs.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not that I am aware of, as the Indians have, through whom they speak and do their business with the officials of the government. That is one reason for the difficulty in applying the Indian Act to the Eskimos. It is merely a matter of administration; we are seeking to take care of these people in times of distress, which fortunately are very infrequent, since they appear to be able to look after themselves fairly well. However, in the summer season, or even any other season of the year, they are liable to travel two or three hundred miles and locate themselves in another place; they have no particular habitations which they call their camping grounds or reserves.
Did I understand the minister to say that the Danish government had made some claim that these people were citizens of Denmark?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No; they have made some claim to territory there. Many years ago a Danish explorer conducted an expedition among the islands south of Melville island and explored some territory there. Some claim has been made to that territory. It is not a very serious matter, and we are attempting to adjust it.

You mean it was a claim for territory?
Mr. STEWART (Edmonton)): Yes.
Not with regard to the citizenship of the people?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 1 carry?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think another section should be substituted for this.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If that is necessary to meet the wishes of my hon. friend it will need to be done in an amendment to the Northwest Territories Act. This is merely designed to take it out of the Indian Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There must be some responsibility somewhere.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
allow me, chapter 103, which deals with the Department of the Interior, states in section 4 that the Minister of the Interior shall have the control and management of the affairs of the Northwest Territories and of the Yukon territory. I think that is wide enough to cover it.
Indian Act Amendment

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is because I doubt whether or not that is wide enough that I brought up this matter, and I understand it was for that reason that the section was put in its present form in 1924. In that year subsection 2 of section 4 was added to meet some doubts which arose over the very point the minister has just brought up.

What is the object of the change; why transfer the control of the Eskimos from the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs to the Commissioner of the Northwest Territories. The Commissioner of the Northwest Territories is the Deputy Minister of the Department of the Interior; both the deputy minister and the minister have their offices in Ottawa, and it seems to me that the Department of Indian Affairs is the proper branch to have control of the Eskimos.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Eskimo question covers a much wider territory than is covered by the Indian question. The Eskimos are all along Coronation gulf and are over in Baffin land, in which country there are no Indians; the Eskimos are found also away to the north on Melville island. This embraces a completely northern territory, in which we have the officers of the Northwest Territories council and of the mounted police, and up to the present time we have found it much more convenient and advantageous to handle the matter in this way. The officers of the Northwest Territories branch and of the mounted police at present are looking after the Eskimos. The officers of the Indian department, while they go down the Mackenzie river, only come in contact with the Eskimos who come to Aklavik on the most westerly side of Coronation gulf. At the present moment all the administration given to the Eskimos is given by the officers of the Northwest Territories and by the mounted police who work very closely together.

Are any schools
being conducted for the education of the Eskimos?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

For instance, in
the duties of the franchise?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is unduly alarmed about this franchise business. That is a matter which can be discussed thoroughly when the bill is introduced to add this territory to the Yukon.

Did I understand the
minister to say that schools similar to the Indian schools will be inaugurated for the Eskimos.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Anglican church has been working among the Eskimos for many years.
That is a private work.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes. The
hon. member will understand that this is a very difficult problem with the tribes moving about as they do, but we have given some thought to the establishment of permanent schools such as we have now for Indian education.
With regard to the Indian schools; what class of teacher is provided, and is any religious instruction given?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Undoubtedly there is religious instruction given in the schools. About 51 per cent of the work carried on by the boarding schools is in the hands of the Oblate order, and the sisters of that order do the teaching. Anglican schools are conducted in the same manner, except that the men and women are hired by the church. The Presbyterian, and formerly the Methodist schools were carried on in the same way, and naturally there is religious instruction given. The curriculum is governed by the provincial laws.

Do I understand that
public funds are being expended for religious instruction?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, I would not say that public funds are being voted for that purpose. The grants are made on the understanding that the schools will be conducted according to the provincial laws, but it would be absolutely wrong to say that no religious instruction is given.

Public grants are made
for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They receive the grants for the purpose of educating the children, yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think the Solicitor
General (Mr. Cannon) has put his finger upon the only contention which we are making at the moment in connection with this matter. He has stated that the Commissioner of the Northwest Territories is not a minister responsible to this house nor to the country, he is a deputy minister who is a paid official of the crown. A minister has responsibility to one or either of the houses of parliament, and inasmuch as in 1924 it was thought desirable that a responsible minister should be charged with the obligation of administering the affairs of the Eskimos, it would seem to

Indian Act Amendment
mo that some designation would be desirable, which would continue the sense of ministerial responsibility.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Previously the Indian Act stated who was responsible for the Eskimos, but we have now an order in council instead of an act of parliament, and my hon. friend has doubts as to whether or not the act covering the Department of the Interior is wide enough.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It was thought it was not in 1924, and it was thought desirable to make it clear that a minister in either house of parliament should be the person responsible for the administration, or shall I say the minister in charge rather than the administrator, because there is a clear distinction between administration and ministerial responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is my intention to ask for an amendment to the Northwest Territories Act. All we are asking here is merely the repealing of what we did in 1927 in regard to the Indian Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This would be the act in which it would appear because they are wards of the nation. After all, the Indian Act is merely a code for dealing with the wards of the nation. They are called Indians in one instance, and Eskimos in another, both aborigines of this country. They are both wards of the nation and they are both covered by the Indian Act, which is a code only to deal with the conduct of the business of the wards of the nation as between the wards and the state. That is the reason I am drawing this point to the attention of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend's convention were right, all that would be necessary to be done would be to add to the subsection that the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, be repealed and that the control be placed under the Minister of the Interior.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Except that it is not usual to deal with a statute in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I confess
that my hon. friend has confused me. I would consider that the Northwest Territories Act would have to be amended. If my hon. friend would allow this section to stand, we will look into it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I desired to make it clear to my hon. friend, as it is a legal matter. Subsection 2 says:
The Superintendent General of Indian Affairs shall have charge of Eskimo affairs.
Instead of a minister we have now an officer, and if it is desired to follow the principle of ministerial responsibility, then there should be a substitution.
Section stands.
On section 2-Annuities and interest applied to maintenance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is a very drastic
change.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It merely
gives us the right to transfer the moneys set aside. The present subsection reads:
The superintendent general may apply the whole or any part of the annuities and interest moneys of Indian children attending an industrial or boarding school to the maintenance of such school or to the maintenance of the children themselves.
It is merely widening the powers. The annuities and interest moneys of Indian children attending industrial or boarding schools are not required for and not applied to the maintenance of such schools, and the provision for such application is eliminated in the amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am sure the minister
realizes the seriousness of the situation. In four or five lines he changes a whole principle in connection with the appropriation of public money. Under the section as it existed before, a school was to be maintained and public funds went to maintain the school. This will enable the department to farm them out, a most pernicious practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is wrong.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
To pay somebody for
them.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: May I explain the difficulty? In the last five years, finding that those boarding schools particularly were in great difficulties financially, we have taken over the schools and their equipment in their entirety and the government have become responsible for them. There is no further charge upon the pupils, the Indians or anyone else for the maintenance of those schools. The teaching of course is still undertaken by the churches, and per capita grants made to assist in the tuition. All we are trying to do is to make applicable to the teaching the annuities that formerly were applied to the maintenance of those schools, sometimes to the construction of them, of course always, I will admit, largely under the control of the tribes themselves. [DOT]
Are the Indians consulted as to the religion they want their children to be taught?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The Indians are always consulted. Seldom if ever do we take a child from an Indian family, unless the family are leading a vicious life, and place it in a school in opposition to their wishes.
Indian Act Amendment
Are they consulted as to the kind of religion they want their children taught ?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Always.

I should like to ask whether a situation like this would not obtain: if some piece of Indian territory or reserve is needed for a public purpose such as a railway, the consent of the band has to be obtained. They are paid so much of the sum, I think it is 50 per cent, in cash and the balance is put into their fund. There is always great difficulty in getting the Indians to sign because they say-"What is the use of our signing? We get only 50 per cent and the other 50 per cent you take and keep. You use it for relief; now you are using it for schools." The government is going to make it more difficult to get Indians to agree to this sort of thing. The interest on the money has been used to pay for relief and the department pays for relief in any case. The next time the Indians are asked to give up land, they will say: "What is the use?
