maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before Your Honour leaves the chair and the house resolves itself into committee of supply, I would like to discuss a question which I consider to be of the utmost importance, and one which should be brought to the attention of parliament. Since the house has been in session, many days have been spent in the discussion of question of importance. We have discussed questions pertaining to butter, to eggs, and to cheese, and while I would not for a moment try to belittle the importance of those matters, I do not think they can compare in importance to the subject I wish to bring to the attention of the house, namely, the unemployment and under-employment which exists at the present time in the Dominion of Canada. Important as this matter is, not a day has been devoted to the discussion of it since parliament met on February 20.
It may be said, and no doubt will be said during the course of this discussion, that this is not a federal question, that it belongs to the provinces and does not concern this House of Commons. But parliament cannot evade its responsibility to the people. If time can be spent in discussing the questions to which I have just referred, then I think we can spend a little time in discussing this important matter. We owe a duty to the men and women who happen to find themselves out of work. It may be said that we have no legal responsibility towards these people. I cannot admit that. I contend that if there is no legal responsibility there is not an hon. member of this house who will say that we have not a moral responsibility in the matter. It will possibly be claimed! that the British North

Unemployment-Mr. Heaps
America Act grants certain jurisdictions and creates certain lines of demarcation between the provincial and the federal governments. I am almost sick and tired of listening to definitions of the British North America Act. Every time a social question of importance is brought before this house the British North America Act is trotted out to show that we cannot do a certain thing. I am beginning to think that instead of calling it the B.N.A. act we should call it the B.A.N. act.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As I have said on a previous occasion, the British North America Act was made for the people of the Dominion of Canada; the people of Canada were not made for the British North America Act.
Within the last few days this house has been very busy in making friendly gestures towards the people to the south of us. I have no objection whatever to friendly gestures being made to people in other parts of the world; in fact as a member of the Labour party I always try to cultivate kindly feelings between the people in different parts of the world. But if we can make friendly gestures which will cost the national exchequer of this country about $10,000,000 per year, then we can afford to make a friendly gesture to the unemployed people in the Dominion of Canada. My constituents are to a very large extent men or women who have to work for wages; if they do not work they cannot eat, and to them this question of unemployment is a very vital one. Am I to go back to my constituents at the end of this session and tell them that parliament sat by idly while they suffered? Am I to tell them that no action is to be taken with regard to this very important question of unemployment? Parliament could well afford to devote its time and energy to doing something for the people of this Dominion in order to alleviate the conditions which some unfortunately now find themselves in. I realize that the government have done something in regard to finding work. I am now accepting the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to a delegation from the western provinces which waited upon him a few days ago when he said that the government was going ahead with public works as fast as it could and that the Canadian National Railways were doing the same-a few men being laid off but otherwise the work proceeding as if everything were normal. That, however, does not begin to touch the question of unemployment in the Dominion. The government have not dealt with unemployment in a direct sense; they have merely pre-
vented it from getting worse than it is at the present time. I want to see parliament take some action that will deal with this question which arises year after year, because hardly a year goes by without this question of unemployment coming before parliament in one form or another.
The average workingman to-day is not the same as the workingman of twenty or thirty years ago. He is beginning to study; he is studying economics and when he is out of work he wants to know the reason why. That is a phase of the matter which we cannot lightly pass over. He sees that all around him are the material things of life. He himself has produced all the things that go towards making life worth while; but suddenly he finds himself out of work; he is face to face with poverty and in many cases does not know where his next meal is to come from. In parliament we protect practically all our industries, all our financial institutions, and the working people would like to know why we cannot give some protection to the workingman. When I use the term "protection" I do not use it in the sense of increased tariffs; I am using it in an entirely different sense. The workingman has the right to security in life in exactly the same way as we give security to capital.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: How does the hon. member propose to do that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will come to that in a few moments if my hon. friend will permit me to continue my argument.
We give, for instance, protection to our railways; we almost guarantee them a certain fixed return on their capital. We give certain concessions to our banks. We give tariff protection to our industries, but what does parliament give to our working people? Practically nothing at all; and to-night as a representative of the working people of Canada I want to try to impress upon parliament the necessity of our doing something on their behalf.
Why, in the first place, is a person employed?-and now I am coming to the answer to some of the questions put by the hon member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine). A person is employed because his services are required in order that the employer may profit from his labour. If a man cannot be gainfully employed, his services are, generally speaking, not required. In periods of depression labour cannot be gainfully employed; hence we have the unemployment problem on our hands. We do not have unemployment periodically as we used to have it many years ago, but it is an ever-recurring problem year after year. Why is it a recurring problem? Years ago it was

Unemployment-Mr. Heaps
claimed that cycles of depression would come once every five or seven years, but with the increasing use of machinery, with the speeding-up process to which labour has been subjected in recent years, production has increased by leaps and bounds and in a very short period during a year we can produce enough to satisfy all human requirements. When I say "enough to satisfy human requirements" I limit that statement by the qualification "in accordance with the purchasing power which the masses happen to possess". It is claimed by economists that during the past twenty years production has approximately doubled, but wages, that is, real wages, have remained almost stationary. That means that the position of the workingman has become relatively worse instead of better. When production becomes greater and greater, when we are able to produce more of the things of life, the position of the workingman should be better, but we find that it is exactly the reverse. At the present time, when we have an over-production of everything, we have the greatest poverty and want and what applies to the workingman applies equally at this time to our farmers. It requires to-day a smaller number of men to produce a given quantity of commodities and that is why less labour is required. As less labour is required, it is only natural that the amount of unemployment prevalent throughout the Dominion should become greater and greater.
In order to overcome the difficulty which confronts us on account of the ever-increasing productivity of the machine and the vast amount of unemployment that prevails in Canada as well as in other parts of the world, two things are required. One is a decreased working day and the other is an increased purchasing power on the part of the masses in order that they may consume more of the commodities which they themselves produce. Even if these two things come about, we shall still have quite an amount of unemployment in Canada.
These two questions cannot by any stretch of the imagination be claimed to be provincial in character. They are national; in fact, I can say they are international in character. Consequently it would be almost absurd for us to expect provincial governments to be able to deal with such questions and I can hardly expect nine provincial governments to deal with them. So far as I am able to judge, the provincial governments have all requested that the federal parliament take some action in regard to the matter. What action can we hope for?
I believe, in spite of its many drawbacks, in spite of its many handicaps, we shall ultimately have to come to a system of unemployment insurance. I cannot for the life of me see how any one particular province can of its own volition, inaugurate within its own boundaries a satisfactory system of unemployment insurance; it is practically impossible for them to do so. I wish, therefore, to deal with the question of unemployment insurance, not only from the aspect of the immediate problem itself, but also having regard to the impression that has gone throughout the country that parliament will do something along that particular line. In 1919 a federal commission was appointed by the then government. This commission had among its members many well known gentlemen, the chairman being the late Mr. Justice Mathers of the province of Manitoba. The commission travelled throughout the length and breadth of Canada, and after taking most voluminous evidence in all part3 of the Dominion, it recommended the following:
We recommend immediate inquiry by expert boards into the following subjects, with a view to early legislation:
(a) State insurance against unemployment, sickness, invalidity and old age.
But ever since the year 1919 nothing has been done in a practical way to implement the recommendations of the royal commission of that year.
In the year 1924, we had hopes that something further was to be done. The Dominion government of that day had a large conference gathered from all parts of the Dominion, sitting at Ottawa, to discuss the question of unemployment. But when the conference had finished its labours nothing further was done.
I have referred earlier in my remarks to the question of interprovincial jurisdiction, and in this connection I should like, if I may, to refer to the platform of the Liberal party in the year 1921. I hope I shall be pardoned for making this reference, but I presume that the party in power to-day have not by any means changed their opinions since this platform was adopted. They issued in October 1921 a small booklet known as Publication No. 7. This is what they had to say in regard to social insurance:
That in so far as may be practicable, having regard to Canada's financial position, an adequate system of insurance against unemployment, sickness, dependence in old age. and other disability, which would include old age pensions, widows' pensions and maternity benefits, should be instituted by the federal government in conjunction with the governments of the several provinces; and that on matters pertaining to industrial and social legislation an
Unemployment-Mr. Heaps

effort should be made to overcome any question of jurisdiction between the Dominion and the provinces by effective cooperation between the several governments.
I heartily subscribe, Mr. Speaker, to that particular clause of the Liberal party platform of 1921.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That was only a chart.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am coming in a moment
to the Conservative chart. I sincerely hope that the government have not gone back on their platform of that year, and that on this question of unemployment insurance they will earnestly endeavour to overcome any difficulty over jurisdiction as between the provinces and the Dominion.
In order to make things even as between the two major parties in this house, I wish to quote from the labour policy adopted by the Conservative party in the city of Winnipeg in November, 1927. I do not know whether it was the environment and bracing air of the city of Winnipeg that impelled our friends of the Conservative party to include this particular clause in their platform. Nevertheless, I am glad to see it there, and I hope that they will stay with it to the bitter end. Section 9 of that platform, dealing with capital and labour, says:
So far as is practicable, to support social legislation designed to conserve human life, health and temperance, to relieve distress during periods of unemployment, sickness and old age; to encourage uniformity in labour laws throughout Canada and the wider spread of technical education, both in industry and agriculture.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
"So far as
is practicable."

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
So far as that little proviso
is concerned, it would not be very difficult to overcome the problem of jurisdiction as between the provinces and the Dominion. I feel satisfied if the two major parties would only attempt to solve this question of jurisdiction it could be solved just as easily as it was in the case of old age pensions. I am sure that exactly the same jurisdiction problem could arise and would have arisen, if anybody had wanted to raise it, in regard to old age pensions. But where there was a will there was a way; the jurisdiction difficulty was overcome, and at the present time, according to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) there are 34,000 aged people in this Dominion drawing the old age pension-This in spite of all jurisdiction difficulties.
The question of unemployment insurance has been raised year after year ever since I have been in this house. This is my fifth session in parliament. In the very first session

that I was here my hon. friend and colleague from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) and I wrote a letter to the present Prime Minister and to the then leader of the opposition. I show you, Mr. Speaker, that the unemployment situation was even then, a very serious one, my colleague and I stressed it as being one of the most important questions with which we thought parliament had to deal. We addressed a very short communication to the two leaders under date of January 7, 1926, as follows:
As representatives of Labour in the House of Commons, may we ask whether it is your intention to introduce, at this session, legislation with regard to (a) provision for the unemployed; (b) old age pensions.
(Signed) J. S. Woodsworth.
A. A. Heaps.
From the right hon. Prime Minister we received a very sympathetic reply, and not many days later, on January 28, 1926, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) had this to say in the House of Commons, in answer to a question from my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill):
This question of unemployment relief is a difficult one in this country owing to the fact that we have a division of powers between federal, provincial and municipal authorities. It has been fdit that the problem primarily is one of local responsibility, but the government is willing in case of serious emergency, when a grave situation exists, to cooperate with the provincial and local authorities, and to bear a share of relief work or other relief measures which have to be adopted to meet a serious situation of that character, and we shall ask parliament to give us authority to that effect.
That was in 1926. If there was a grave emergency as regards unemployment in the early part of the winter of 1926, the emergency in 1930 is a great deal more grave than it was four years ago; and if the emergency of 1926 prompted the federal government to give assistance to the municipal bodies and provincial governments, there is a thousand times more reason for giving that assistance to-day. I think I am correctly interpreting the intentions of the government as then expressed when I say that this was only a temporary measure of relief, looking forward to a more definite scheme dealing with the whole question of unemployment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask how many unemployed there are in the city of Winnipeg to-day, and how many are on part time?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is almost impossible for
me to say definitely how many people in Winnipeg are at present out of work or only partly employed. The figures vary-some say ten thousand; some say more. According to

Unemployment-Mr. Heaps
statements that I have heard made by people who are competent to judge, ten thousand would not be exaggerating the situation so far as Winnipeg and its immediate surburbs are concerned.
Further, Mr. Speaker, in 1927 I introduced a motion for a committee to go into the question of unemployment insurance. Unfortunately some of my hon. friends opposite were very talkative on that occasion, and the discussion was not concluded at six o'clock, so that the motion went to the bottom of the order paper and could not again be discussed during that session. But in 1928 we had a committee appointed by this house to deal with the question of unemployment insurance. What did that committee report? I am going to read just one clause:
That the evidence of the justice department makes it clear that the responsibility for such legislation rests on the provincial authorities, it being within their jurisdiction under the provisions of the British North America Act, but that it would be within the power of parliament to contribute by grant to such provinces as adopted such legislation, following the precedent set in the matter of technical education, highway construction, and, more recently the Old Age Pensions Act.
In other words, when the committee reported in 1928 it claimed that parliament was competent to make grants to any system of unemployment insurance in exactly the same way as at the present time we make grants to the system of old age pensions adopted by many of the provinces.
But we come to 1929, last year, when again the same resolution was submitted to the committee on industrial and international relations. Their report considerably whittled down the report of the year previous. Let me quote this paragraph:
Your committee recognizes that, while it is highly desirable that such legislation should be uniform in all the provinces, and while social insurance has a federal aspect, nevertheless according to the Department of Justice under our constitution legislative jurisdiction in relation to the establishment of a compulsory system of unemployment insurance is vested exclusively in the provincial legislatures.
Not a word about the right of this parliament to make grants to the provincial governments in order to assist the establishment of unemployment insurance in the Dominion. The report also contained the following:
That the federal government be requested to bring the subject matter of this reference before the next federal-provincial conference, and your committee suggests when the agenda for such a conference is being arranged that the provincial governments be invited to send representatives of the employer and employee to discuss the subject matter of this report.
Now, Mr. Speaker, any ordinary person reading that section of the report would be under the impression that it was the intention of parliament to do something in regard to the question of unemployment insurance and in some way give relief to persons who happen to be out of work.
During last winter two conferences were called in Winnipeg to deal with the question of unemployment in western Canada. One conference was called in November, and the other in January. As a result of those conferences a delegation came from western Canada to Ottawa and interviewed the government. In a statement which the right hon. Prime Minister made to this delegation the impression was broadcast that the government was sympathetic and willing to do something to speed forward unemployment insurance. This is what he is reported to have said according to the Ottawa Evening Citizen of February 27:
Eventually Canada will have a system of unemployment insurance. This was the only constructive way to deal with the unemployment situation and be hoped it would soon be possible to work out an insurance plan. Seasonal measures in the way of relief and public works were of no permanent assistance and an insurance plan offered the only constructive way of avoiding distress. Under it those who employed them would be compelled to contribute to a fund during their periods of employment and the insured would receive benefits when out of work.
A statement of this character, Mr. Speaker, would give an impression particularly to the working people of Canada, that the government had it in mind to deal with this question, which we regard as one of the most vital confronting the Dominion at the present time. A few days later my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre asked a question of the right hon. Prime Minister in relation to his statement made to the delegation, and in his answer he seemed to some extent to retract -if I may use the term-something of what he had said a few days previously:	I quote
the question and answer:
Mr. Woodsworth:	As I understaud the
statement, it was to the effect that the federal government was very much concerned in the matters of unemployment and believed that one of the solutions was a system of unemployment insurance, and that the government would be willing to take any steps possible towards bringing about an understanding between the provinces and the federal government. I want to know if the government would be willing to undertake the calling of a special conference so that this matter can be expedited.
Mr. Mackenzie King:	My recollection is that
a special committee of this house considered this question last session and brought to the house a renort to the effect that unemployment
Unemployment-Mr. Heaps

insurance was necessarily a matter with which provincial governments rather than the federal government would have to deal. I think I expressed the view yesterday that in my opinion a system of unemployment insurance would be a constructive way to deal with the unemployment problem, to which system not only the employer and the governments concerned would contribute, but the worker also. If the provinces make a move in this matter and it appears that the federal government can be of assistance in helping to bring about uniformity as between the provinces of any plan proposed, or can cooperate in other ways in any discussion on the subject, we shall be glad upon invitation to take the matter under consideration.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think this statement of the Prime Minister went far enough; it contained too many reservations. First of all, he states that he is prepared to discuss this question with the provinces on an invitation from them. I claim, sir, that it should be the duty of the federal government to bring about a conference with the provincial governments. He cannot expect nine provincial governments to call the federal government into consultation. I think it would be far easier and would show more sympathetic consideration on the part of the government if they themselves called the nine provincial governments into conference to discuss the question. He also said that this is primarily a provincial question. I have always refused to admit that, and I claim the federal government have just as much responsibility in respect to this question as any of our provincial governments, in fact their responsibility is greater.
Now I want to go a little further and come to a statement made more recently. I turn to my good friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan). On the 14th day of March he made a speech in the city of London, Ontario, and evidently it was a very good speech. I want to thank him for it, because on asking a question of him a couple of days subsequently he told me to read the London Advertiser and he would stand behind everything he said on that particular occasion as there reported. In compliance with the invitation extended to me by the Minister of Labour, I am going to read extracts from his London speech. Evidently the people of London thought it was a^ very good one, and I shall read what the London Advertiser thought of it. In its columns I find the following:
Mr. Heenan, in a powerful address full of practical illustrations drawn from his daily contact with the problems of the worker and spiced with wit and humour, held the attention of an enthusiastic audience.

In that moment of exuberance, and with the enthusiastic backing of an audience of workers in the city of London, he spoke thus:
I believe during the times of depression the workers have some claim to a portion of the profits made by their labour during favourable years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: What is that statement?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, that is what appears
here.
In a word, I believe, as the Prime Minister stated in his book entitled Industry and Humanity, "where the interests of industry and humanity conflict, industry must give way."
I quite agree with the statements of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour. To continue with the quotations:
So I believe that the time has come when the employers and the workers, and if necessary the governments, should contribute to a fund in order to provide insurance against unemployment.
I feel when the Minister of Labour made that statement to the working people of the city of London he had in mind the federal government, as well as the provincial government. The quotation further states:
A system could be inaugurated in this country which would be suitable to Canadian needs.
Remember, he says "Canadian needs," not provincial needs.
Take, for example, our Canadian railroad workers; in the summer time there are upwards of two hundred thousand men employed, and during the winter periods there are about twenty-five thousand of those workers laid off for several months. The wages of all railway-men average about $130 per month.
I must say that I do not agree with that statement. According to my information, and from reading an examination of the figures furnished by our Labour department and the bureau of statistics I find that the average wage paid by railroads in this country, from the highest to the lowest, is about 55 or 56 cents per hour. Further, I know cases in the city of Winnipeg where railwaymen have kept a check of the higher scaled trades, such as machinists, and they tell me the average monthly pay was $113. When you consider that there are men working on the railroad for 35 or 45 cents an hour, you will realize that there must be vast numbers whose average wage is not over $15 a week. However, I shall read further:
This would not be too hard on either and if necessary, the governments could assist.
I agree with him in this respect. His next statement is:

Unemployment-Mr. Heaps
This system could be extended to workers in every industry and would provide a permanent system.
I agree with that. Unemployment insurance would provide a permanent system whereby men who happened to be out of work would not have to go begging. They would have an insurance fund to fall back upon, the same as exists in other parts of the world. At this juncture I want to point out that although it would be better for the unemployed, a system of unemployment insurance will not cure the problems of unemployment. The minister continued:
The workers of Canada are entitled to a permanent system. The House of Commons unanimously has already endorsed such a system. Parliament has also declared it is a provincial matter, and the government has taken the matter up with the provinces, hut notwithstanding the fact that it is a provincial obligation the Prime Minister has stated that if the provinces so desire his government is prepared to cooperate with them in establishing a uniform system.
The last statement is rather significant, and in my view very important. I am in favour of uniform legislation when it comes down to social questions. I do not believe the people of one province should be treated better or worse than the people of a neighbouring province. It is so in the case of the Old Age Pensions Act. This parliament was anxious to have uniform legislation, and so far as uniformity is concerned I do not think anybody would agree to repeal that legislation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman whether he intends to conclude his remarks by moving an amendment?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, I intend to move an amendment in a few minutes. The Minister of Labour went on to say:
As far as I am concerned, I will make every effort and the Prime Minister will hack me up to see that the labouring man who is out of work for any period of the year will have a right to expect and to receive a share of the profits he helped to make.
I believe when the Minister of Labour made this statement to the people of the city of London, Ontario, he had in mind that the federal parliament would compel employers of labour to contribute something out of their profits towards an unemployment insurance scheme. In the speech to which the Minister of Labour directed my attention there is no place in which he states that it is entirely a provincial matter or that the federal government would not assume its responsibility with regard to it. If I am to make an exact interpretation of the minister's speech I would say it meant that the federal government was
prepared to proceed with a scheme of federal unemployment insurance. Not only that, but it would indicate that the federal government would see to it that the scheme was uniform throughout the length and breadth of Canada. Uniformity of this character is absolutely essential in a plan involving unemployment insurance, just as it is in the case of old age pensions. It would be impossible to have a system of unemployment insurance confined to any particular province; such a system would have to be operative in at least five of the provinces before it could become workable in Canada.
I do not wish to say much more, Mr. Speaker, in regard to what has been said out of the house by members of the government. I would like to make one or two comments, however, in regard to parliament itself. We have been discussing questions in this house for the past five or six weeks which touch only a very small proportion of the people of this country. There is no question which affects Canadians so vitally as does that of unemployment and under employment. In this country at the present time I would say there must be one hundred thousand people suffering from the effects of these two conditions. Let each man who is unemployed be said to represent three people, we have a total of three hundred thousand people who are suffering, three hundred thousand people who want to know what parliament intend to do in connection wth this very important question.
There is another problem involved in this matter of unemployment insurance. To-day a man's security in bis employment is not nearly what it was fifteen or twenty years ago. He never knows when some new invention or some new piece of machinery will be brought into the factory to take his place. I venture to say that if a proper census could be taken of the turnover of labour in industry it would show a greater number than we realize at the present time. I know figures have been presented in this house to show that more people are employed in industry now than were employed five or six years ago, but even those figures do not present an actual picture of the state of affairs. What I should like to know is how many hours people have been employed in industry over a given period. There we might find a different story. I believe the index figure for March 1 was about 106; there was a considerable reduction from February 1. It may be possible to show that that figure of 106 compares favourably with the figure of perhaps 95 ten years ago, but it might be shown also that the 95 figure means more hours than the 106. Our bureau
Unemployment-Mr. Heaps

of statistics does not give us any data on that important feature of our employment situation in Canada. For instance, we know that in the railroad shops and in many other subsidiary industries men were laid off not by hundreds but by thousands, yet these men were part of those employed during 1929 and perhaps part of those employed during 1930. The result is that although the index number is higher, not knowing the number of hours these men worked during the year we cannot get an accurate picture of the situation.
The federal government, in conjunction with the provincial governments, spent a great deal of money in collecting these statistics, yet we have no way of finding out how may men are out of employment in Canada. We have some idea of how many men are employed, but there are no figures to show how many men are unemployed. One of the officials of the Department of Labour has said that when there is the greatest number of men out of work there are the fewest registrations with the employment bureaus or, as I sometimes call them, the unemployment bureaus. That is so because the men claim there is no use going to these places because there is no work for them. So we have no means of knowing how great our unemployment problem may be, except from the relief which is extended by our municipal authorities, and if we gauge the unemployment situation this year by the relief extended by our municipal and provincial authorities it will be seen that this is one of the worst unemployment years we have had in this Dominion for twenty years past.
This is not a problem which comes occasionally, perhaps once every ten or fifteen years. It is an annual problem, and I feel that this house will be derelict in its duty if we do not take some definite action in order to deal with what is obviously a great national question. The Minister of Justice stated that a nemergency existed ini the year 1926. If that was so, the emergency is very much greater this year, and the problem of unemployment should not be passed over in this house year after year. Hon. members should not be required to get up in- their places and ask the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour what they intend doing about the unemployment situation, only to be told that it is a provincial problem. It is my contention, Mr. Speaker, that a problem which affects the well-being of the people of this country is a federal problem. If pigs or cattle in any province of this Dominion became sick, our Department of Agriculture would send expert after expert and spend federal money freely in order to find out the cause and cure of that

illness, but when we have human beings suffering, we are told it is not a federal question. I should like to know how long a human being has not been considered an equally valuable asset as a cow or a pig.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member one question if I may. What countries have social insurance legislation at present?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It would take a long time to enumerate them all, but I might point out that South Africa was one of the last dominions to adopt legislation of this kind. In 1926 the government of South Africa appointed a commission to inquire into the question of social insurance, and that commission reported in favour of old age pensions, sickness, invalidity and unemployment insurance. All those recommendations were adopted with the exception of unemployment insurance, and if I am not mistaken the recommendation dealing with unemployment insurance was one of the last parts of that report to be adopted as a federal measure. I believe that in Australia they have had similar insurance as a provincial measure, but now in that country they are considering bringing in a federal measure in order to do away with the question of provincial jurisdiction. When a dominion such as South Africa, sparsely populated and with conditions very much akin to those existing here-and the same could be said with regard to Australia-has adopted insurance of this kind as a federal measure, there is no reason in the world why this federal parliament should not follow such a lead.
In Europe most countries have schemes of this character. Great Britain has had unemployment insurance since 1911, and although different commissions have inquired into the question of this insurance, the last being the Blanesburgh commission, whose report was published in 1925, they have all found in favour of social insurances. The last report stated in effect that social insurance had become an integral part of the social structure of the British Isles. Why Canada should be more backward than the other parts of the British Empire is something I do not know. If every other part of this commonwealth of nations has adopted social insurance generally as a federal responsibility, there is no reason why this parliament should not do the same thing through this federal government, just as we did with regard to old age pensions.
I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that the working people of this country were beginning to study these problems; they are trying to understand these economic questions and are taking an interest in the activities of both

Unemployment-Mr. Adshead
federal and provincial parliaments. To them unemployment is the important question. When we go back to our constituents they say to us, "What have you done as a member of parliament on the question of the unemployment situation?" The reply will be: "We have not done anything, because .some question of interprovincial jurisdiction has arisen and it is contended that is not our sphere." They will go then to the provincial member, who will say, "We have discussed this question in the provincial legislature and we think the federal government should assume responsibility for this matter because it is federal in character." There we have the passing of the buck as between one government and another. What will the average workingman have to say? We have a responsibility in this regard and if we do not desire to bring parliament and democratic government into disrepute, this parliament should act in the interests of the common people. Can any hon. member go back to his constituency and face his electors and honestly say that because of some question of jurisdiction parliament refuses to assume responsibility?
We hope that when the hon. Minister of Labour and the right hon. the Prime Minister take part in this debate they will measure up to their responsibilities and not be afraid to say that parliament owes a certain duty to the people of the Dominion of Canada. I hope that the hundreds of thousands of people who are looking towards this House of Commons will not be disappointed in the discussion which is to follow and can look forward to some action by the ministers of the crown.
For these reasons, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland):
That all the words after "that" be struck out, and the following be substituted:
"in the opinion of this house the government should take immediate action to deal with the question of unemployment."
Mr. PI B. ADSHEAD (East Calgary): Mr. Speaker, I think it devolves upon all Labour members of the house to take part in the discussion of a question of this kind. First of all, I wish to comment somewhat along the lines adopted by the hon. member who has just moved this resolution (Mr. Heaps), when he quoted the remarks of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) in a speech delivered at London. The minister was not giving utterance to a mere pious wish or sentiment when he said:
T will utilize my every effort and the premier will back me up to see that the labouring man who is out of work for any period of the year will have a right to expect and to receive a share of the profits he helped make.
That was the statement of a responsible minister of this country-that the government would do something along the line of unemployment insurance. It cannot be regarded as a personal wish or personal statement of a minister of the crown when he said that the Prime Minister himself was with him in the matter. The Minister of Labour has made no denial or rebuttal of that statement, and so we can regard it as being correct. He went on to say:
The workers who are unemployed

Not only does he go on to say this himself, but he is speaking for the government and it is responsible for his statement. He said:
The workers who are unemployed for perhaps two or three months of the year constituted an essential unit in the industrial life of the nation for the remaining period and the country should recognize their rights.
He went on to say:
Those who oppose progress and social legislation of any kind will call it the dole. It is not that. It is a measure of protection to which the workers are entitled.
The Minister of Labour laid out a course which was to be followed by the government, and the Prime Minister has given his assent. I hope that the minister and the Prime Minister will have something to say in this debate, and relieve the house of any doubt it may have as to what the minister said.
At times I have been twitted in this house, especially by my hon. friends to my right, of being more liberal in my practices than I should be; in fact the hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Spence) said the other day that I should be on the other side of the house. I have great pleasure in referring to some of the Liberal principles which were enunciated in 1919, and which should revive the drooping spirits of those Liberals who remained true to Liberalism. I suppose there are a few who stiil stand by the principles enunciated in that year when they were in opposition. There is an old saying:
When the devil was sick, the devil a saint would be,
But when the devil was well, the devil a bit cared he.
I have no desire to apply that principle to my hon. friends across the house, but when parties are out of office they are very apt to make some very fine declarations and state-

Unemployment-Mr. Adshead
ments to catch the ear of the country and after they have been in power for some time they appear to forget them. Many things said in conventions are forgotten in the house. I would like to quote a few things said at that memorable convention in 1919, made memorable by the fact that the Prime Minister made some very nice speeches and presented some excellent resolutions. Speaking to the question of labour, the Prime Minister made this statement:
The guiding principle that labour should not be regarded as a commodity or article of commerce-
That is, that labour is not a thing to be bought and sold, that it is something more than a commodity. That was the first statement of my hon. friend the Prime Minister, and then he went on to state the various proposals which the Liberal party were going to bring into effect after they assumed the reins of office. The Prime Minister went on to say:
That in so far as may be practicable, having regard for Canada's financial position, an adequate system of insurance against unemployment,-
That is the very thing the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) was talking about, and is the very thing about which the minister spoke in the city of London. Some ten years save elapsed since these words were uttered by the Prime Minister:
*-sickness, dependence in old age, and other disability, which would include old age pensions, widows' pensions, and maternity benefits, should be instituted by the federal government in conjunction with the governments of the several provinces;-
I would like my hon. friends on the other side of the house to notice particularly that when the Prime Minister was speaking in 1919 he did not seem to have any idea that difficulty would be met in getting over the British North America Act. He went on to say:
-and that on matters pertaining to industrial and social legislation an effort should be made to overcome any question of jurisdiction between the Dominion and the provinces by effective cooperation between the several governments.
At that time the Prime Minister seemed to think that any obstacle offered by the British North America Act to social legislation could be very easily overcome.
