speechtext:
Do I understand the hon.
member to say that the Prime Minister declared in 1919 that labour was not a commodity to be sold on the market?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am simply quoting what the Prime Minister said, that labour should not be regarded as a commodity or as an article of commerce.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: It cannot be said that labour is a commodity on the market.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I suppose they are going to take such steps as will make it not a commodity.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Have those steps been
taken?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member had
better ask the Prime Minister. Let me quote something further. Speaking to these excellent resolutions which were introduced, the Prime Minister said:
The Liberal party of Canada, in accepting this program in its entirety to-night, is taking a position which, in the course of time, will be regarded as historic; it is declaring itself the first political party in any country in the world to accept this program, and to ask its followers to join with other nations in carrying it out.
That was ten years ago.
Not only does the resolution recognize that the labour problem is a world problem.
I want to commend that statement to my hon. friends on the other side. It is not a provincial problem; it is not even solely a national problem; it is according to the Prime Minister, a world problem. He goes on:
It recognizes also that the labour problem is a human problem. The resolution is based on the assumption that human personality is more important than any considerations of property. It is founded on the belief that ethical and human considerations ought to stand above considerations which are purely business or material.
Then follows a very expressive sentence which I wish we could live up to more fully:
It is an expresion of the belief-
That was the Prime Minister's belief and I hope it is still.
-that industry exists for the sake of humanity, not humanity for the sake of industry.
I might quote a good deal more in that connection, but I think I have given enough to show the point of view from which my friends of the Liberal party and the Prime Minister were looking at the matter of unemployment insurance and many other pieces of social legislation which he proposed to introduce when the party got into power. Of that social legislation all we have is the old age pension, which was obtained after a good deal of struggle. I 'hope what I have said to-night will help to revive the memories of those pious declarations.

Unemployment-Mr. Adshead
In connection with the question of unemployment itself, as early as December last I wired to the Prime Minister as follows:
Unemployment here acute but most certainly it is right and just that federal government should bear cost of unemployed destitute immigrants of 1929 brought out by Immigration department. I have asked this for three years.
And then, referring to the conditions in the city of Calgary at that particular time, I said:
Churches fed 275 at dinner to-day, not all immigrants. Those immigrants awaiting deportation should be speedily dealt with but cost of their maintenance should not be borne by city or private people.
Unemployment in Calgary was acute at that particular time, and I received a letter today stating that the unemployment situation there at present is serious. To show how acute unemployment was at that time and is even now, I may say that the men who were fed were not the only ones out of employment, but they were men who were actually starving, who had nothing to eat and nowhere to lie. The first persons who took the matter up were the ladies of the Labour party in Calgary, and they fed 200 men. The next who took it up were the women of the Conservative League of the city of Calgary who undertook for a week to feed 300 men. The number had begun to increase. After they had done this for a week, the ladies of the Liberal League took it up and they fed these 300 men for another week. Finally the matter became so acute that the churches took it up.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Did they all give it up?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not know. They carried on the work at least as far as their finances would permit, and the question became so serious that they asked me to wire not only the Prime Minister but the Immigration department and the Labour department. I think the Minister of Labour received a telegram pointing out the seriousness of the unemployment situation in Calgary at that particular time. So far did the question of unemployment and destitution go that our good policemen in the station of the Canadian Pacific allowed these men as far as they could to sleep in the smoking room and about the station until such time as they were compelled to turn them out into the cold. Then, with the thermometer at twenty below zero, the men went into the streets with their coat collars turned up and got into any niche in which they could to find shelter for the night. Even a minister of that city telephoned to me saying: "I am sending some men up to you. I have kept them as long as I could. I have allowed them to sleep in 2419-72
the study of my church, and now as you are member for East Calgary, I am going to send them to you to see what you can do." Being member for East Calgary I did what I could. The citizens of Calgary have had to bear a burden which rightfully belongs to the federal government and perhaps to the provincial government.
I notice the following in the press, and I should like to ask the Minister of Labour whether he is acquainted with this fact, if it is a fact:
Ottawa, January 20.-Immigration to Canada of continentals of south and southeastern Europe, that is to say of single men, will be limited this year to 8,000.
An arrangement has been made allocating 4.000 of these each to Canadian Pacific and Canadian National.
I want to know whether this is intended to increase unemployment, or where these 8,000 men are going. My experience has been that upon arriving in the city of Calgary after the prorogation of parliament, I have found a large number of these men taking work right in the city and swelling the number of the unemployed. I can give some statements in this regard. Last year, I think it was, I was standing on the street and I saw a number of men, evidently foreigners-or at least men who could not speak the English language; I do not know whether or not all men who cannot speak English are foreigners. I wondered what they were talking about. They were close to the employment bureau and apparently one of them could speak English. I went over and asked them what the trouble was. These men were recent immigrants, brought into Alberta by the railway companies under conditions which I have just read. We were told by the then Acting Minister of Immigration that there were ploughs and teams waiting for every man who came in; that they were all going to work on the farms and that none of them would work in the cities. He assured me time and again that conditions of employment in the cities would not be in the least affected by the thousands of men who were brought in. I took these men into the Dominion Labour Bureau and took with me a copy, sworn to as to its accuracy, of the document they were reading. They had been under the impression-and the document bore it out-that they were to be engaged by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for at least two months to work on the extra gangs there at thirty cents an hour. In order that the railway company might be quite sure of its position, it got each man to

Unemployment-Mr. Adshead

sign this document, which I will read; because they could not understand how it was that after being engaged for two months they were all discharged after working for three weeks, and another bunch were hired to work on the extra gang. This is the document:
Contract to work made by the undersigned with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Particulars as to work:
(a)	Capacity in which engaged.-Extra gang.
(b)	Locality.-Beddington.
(c)	Rate of wages of actual work.-30 cents per hour.
(d)	Board.-$6 per week.
(e)	Transportation.-Free one way.
(f)	Deductions-medical fee.-$1.50 a month.
(g)	Duration of work.-Two months.
That was the item which these immigrants could not understand. They could not realize why they should not have two months' work when the document stated two months. But there was a little joker in the deck, as there generally is with labour contracts of that sort. It goes on to say:
1.	I declare that I am competent to work in the capacity described above, and if not found competent by the foreman in charge I agree to accept such work as such foreman finds me capable of, at the ruling rate of wages of the company for such work, in the locality mentioned above.
2.	I agree to work for a period of not less than the probable duration of work as set out above (two months).
Now comes the joker. These men were foreigners who did not understand and could not speak the English language. Here is the joker clause:
I agree that no notice of termination of my engagement shall be required to be given by the company.
So they agree to work for two months, if required, and if the company does not want them, they can discharge them at any time. After three weeks' work these men were discharged and helped to swell the ranks of the unemployed in the city of Calgary. Further, I want to draw attention to the binding nature of this agreement and to the penalties that were to be exacted if the men did not live up to it. The following clause was added, and no doubt was very fully explained to the men who were engaged:
Extract from the ordinance respecting master and servants, section 2:
"Any person engaged, bound or hired whether as clerk, journeyman apprentice, servant, labourer or otherwise howsoever guilty of drunkenness or of absenting himself day or night without leave from his proper service or employment or of refusing or neglecting to perform his just duties or to obey the lawful commands of his master or of dissipating his employer's property or effects, shall be deemed 
guilty of a violation of his contract, and upon summary conviction of one or more of the said violations forfeit and pay such sum of money not exceeding $30 as to the justice or magistrate seems meet, together with the costs of the prosecution; and in default thereof forthwith shall be imprisoned for any period not exceeding one month unless the fine imposed and costs, together with the costs of commitment and conveying such person to the place of imprisonment, be sooner paid."

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Why not crucify them at once?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No doubt. I am quoting from a sworn copy of the agreement, and it was no doubt impressed on these men that if they did not work for the full two months, if required, they would be liable to fine or imprisonment. But the company had the right to discharge them at any time they liked. So I ask the Minister of Labour: What are the conditions under which these eight thousand men are coming out to Canada this spring? According to the notice, they start to come about first of March. Are these immigrants, the bringing in of whom by the railways has been sanctioned by the government, going to work on the farm? Are they going where the government supposes they will go, or will their cases be just a repetition of those I have just cited? As soon as I go back to Calgary shall I find these men engaged in work at far less wages than the average worker will accept, thus aggravating the unemployment situation?
I want to give further proof of my statement that when these men come in with a guarantee that they are going to work on the farm, the government, or the Immigration department, which is the same thing, do not know where they are going. Unless some complaint is made, unless somebody draws attention to the fact that these men are not where they should be, the department takes no steps to see that they go where they are supposed to go. I have in my hand a letter that confirms exactly what I have said. Here was a man who was brought out to work on a farm. He signed to go on a farm, the same way that all these men I have spoken of signed to go on a farm. But he never left the city of Calgary, and the Immigration department knew nothing at all about his whereabouts or what he was doing until his case was brought to their attention. This man also helped to swell the ranks of the unemployed. I wrote to the department with a view to getting him deported, after he had been in the city of Calgary for two years. I wish to read the reply I got, and it shows conclusively that the department did not

Unemployment-Mr. Adshead
know where this man was or what he was doing, although he had been brought out to go on a farm. The department said:
Our records show that this man came to Canada to work on the farm. Our records show further that he was brought up on a farm, is fully experienced, and was accompanied to Canada by his wife, a twenty-one year old son, a fifteen year old son, and two smaller children. The two older boys were said to be experienced at farm work. There is no reason at all why this man and his family should not by now have become well on the way to a successful settlement on the land.
Certainly if he had been on the farm for two years, and had had previous experience in farming, there should be no reason why he should not be well settled on the land at the end of that time. The letter continues:
But I take it from your letter that he has been at city work and presumably has not made any effort along agricultural lines. However, we will deal with the case.
Four or five weeks later that man was deported. He had been maintained at the city's expense. What I want to bring out is the fact that that man came out with his wife and family to farm. The department knew that he came out to farm, and stated that he would be placed on a farm, but after having made that statement they knew nothing whatever of his whereabouts or what he was doing until I wrote to them that he had been in the city of Calgary for two years, and asked to have him deported because he was useless and was adding to the ranks of the unemployed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
WThat country did he come
from?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think he came from the old country. His name was John Kidd.
There is another complaint which I have in connection with the unemployment situation, although I understand that the government are not going to grant any more assisted passages. In the past these assisted immigrants have helped to swell the ranks of the unemployed. They come out here supposedly to go on the farms, but they finally land up in the cities. I have a list here of twenty men, farm immigrants, who in the months of December came into the city of Calgary. Some of them got jobs, others tried to get jobs; others joined the ranks of the unemployed and had to get relief from the city. In order to have some of these men deported I asked the city authorities to give them city relief for a week because the Immigration department absolutely refuse to consider deporting these men until they become a public charge. So we had to resort to that expedient before I could apply to the Immigration department to 2419-72i
have them deported. In the meantime, of course, they were swelling the ranks of the unemployed, while others of them were taking work that Canadians resident in the city should have had. I wrote to the Immigration department, and also wired to the Prime Minister to the same effect, asking that some recompense be made to the city and to those who had maintained these men for periods varying from a week to six weeks and two months, and I got this standard reply from the department. It is a peculiar reply, and I would like the Minister of Labour to take note of it. We asked the department to reimburse us the cost of looking after these men whom we were not instrumental in bringing to this country, but the department denied all responsibility. We had to expend several thousand dollars on relief measures. To every such request this is the stock answer we get. It would be humourous but for the tragic circumstances. This is the stereotyped reply:
I venture to suggest that the amount of money spent by the city of Calgary in a few cases-
That is, these numerous immigrants.
-is comparatively small, and further that the same is infinitesimal as compared with the benefit which your city must derive from these immigrants who locate within its borders.
The benefit which we have received from these trainees, these men who came out to farm but eventually landed in our city and finally had to be deported!

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Who signed that letter?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is signed by F. C.
Blair, and is dated December 29, last year. I said it was a stock answer, and this is confirmed by another letter which I received. In fact one would imagine that the form was typed and pasted on the wall for use whenever a request is received by the department from a municipality for reimbursement of money spent on stranded immigrants. The other letter is signed by Mr. Egan. Let me quote it:
I venture to suggest-
The same wording precisely.
-that the amount of money spent by the city of Calgary in a few such cases is comparatively small, and further that the same is infinitesimal as compared with the benefit which your city must derive from these immigrants who locate within its borders.
Both Mr. Egan and Mr. Blair use the same
stereotype form.
I thoroughly agree with the statement of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister that humanity does not exist for industry, but that industry exists for the sake of humanity; that

Unemployment-Mr. Adshead
the human element is the most important. He took the human side of the question. But it is just the lack of that human side which causes the trouble we have in connection with unemployment. For instance, in the city of Calgary last year-and this is typical of many such cases throughout the Dominion-the Canadian Pacific Railway Company without a moment's notice, without any consideration for -their employees, without any consultation with them, discharged them, and those men are still in the city of Calgary without employment and in distress. Now, in view of this and similar cases I ask the Prime Minister, what does he think about labour not being a commodity when great corporations are allowed to discharge their men because they know that in the spring they can get a fresh supply? Those veiy corporations take excellent care of their machines, simply because they regard them as far more valuable than their workmen.
I submit, sir, that it is the duty of the government to implement their promises made in the platform of 1919, even though nine years have elapsed since that platform was published to the Dominion. I trust the Minister of Labour will put his best foot forward to have those promises implemented. Indeed, I think it is up to the government to state to the house how they intend to give effect to the speech made by my hon. friend the Minister of Labour at London, for as a responsible minister of the crown that speech of his is binding on his colleagues in the cabinet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel it is of the utmost importance to each province of the Dominion that we should consider the causes of unemployment. My hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) said that unemployment is not only provincial, it is a federal matter. I believe that it is also an international matter, because it has been studied even by the League of Nations. I see my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) laughing. Let me assure him that unemployment is too serious a matter to laugh at, and I am surprised to see my young friend, who is a man of intelligence, laugh at so serious a problem-a problem that cannot be solved by jokes or laughter. During the past winter I noticed in the New York Times a very sad picture which I place at the disposal of every hon. member. Underneath it is printed the following :
The unemployed of Australia start a slave market. Men out of work in Sydney offer themselves to the lowest bidder in an effort to find employment for themselves.

It discloses a situation infinitely worse than that which prevails here. I wonder if my friend from Queens-Lunenburg could get a fair price for his services in Australia.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: If the hon. member is referring to me, I may say I was laughing at him, not at the problem of unemployment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
When my hon. friend
laughs it makes a general disturbance in the house. In all countries, Mr. Speaker, the social order must be preserved, and any disturbance in that order affects the whole structure. We all remember the great economic disturbance following the war during the period of readjustment. Gradually the world got back to normal. But there is another disturbance of the social order, a continuing disturbance, caused by the shift of our rural population to the cities. People who live happily in the country are attracted by the mirage-like lure of the big cities, and they leave their healthful country surroundings for a stuffy tenement in the city. When those people, either through lack of initiative or of qualifications, fail to find work they become very much embarrassed and eventually are a source of trouble to the community. Then again the constant improvement in machinery displaces more and more men, still further aggravating the unemployment problem. The increased power of our modern freight and passenger engines means that a single train crew can do the work which a few years ago, with the lighter motive power then in use, would have given work to many more train crews.
There is yet another cause of unemployment. In this country we have what are called international unions. I must say that I am in favour of national unions, or Canadian unions. I spoke of the Canadian spirit in this house the other day and arising out of that I ask you how those union heads, who reside in the United States, could have the interests of Canadians at heart. International unions, as a whole, cannot show the Canadian spirit that we may expect from local organizations. What is the effect of unions of an international nature? The effect is that when they have not enough men within their ranks to attend to the work they have in hand, they call people in from the United States to do that work, merely because they are members of the unions, and thereby they discriminate against our Canadian citizens. To my mind this is an incorrect practice, and if something could be done to improve the conditions in this respect it would be highly beneficial to the community. It constitutes the worst kind

Unemployment-Mr. Poulvot
of discrimination. We have people who can do a certain type of work; they are able workers, but camnot obtain employment because they do not belong to a union. Instead of giving employment to Canadians the union leaders call in men from the United States.
I think theTe should be more humanity, not only in industry but in labour, so that such things could be prevented in the future.
The Prime Minister, the Minister of Labour and their colleagues are very much interested in the welfare of the working men of this country. The Prime Minister was the editor of the first number of the Labour Gazette. He has been deputy minister and Minister of Labour, and he has taken great interest in all labour questions. May I say to my hon. friend the Minister of Labour, who has risen from the ranks, that it is a great compliment to organized labour when the head of a government consults labour as to a representative from its ranks to act as a minister in the cabinet. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour is equal to his task, and I am glad to see in this evening's papers that the government is doing its part to fulfil the treaty with respect to labour to the extent of recommending the universal adoption of an eight-hour working day in Canada. An order in council is being introduced to-day, as we have noticed in the papers, to the effect that the government employees will not work more than eight hours a day, and will receive pay for overtime after eight hours' work has been performed. It is because we have such real and sincere friends of labour in the government that the Prime Minister said to the president and chairman of the board of the Canadian National Railways that even if the expenditure was higher, the men who have been working for some time for the Canadian National Railways should continue to be given work. The same instructions have been given with regard to the Department of Public Works, and we find the Acting Minister of Imimgration (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) stating that subsidies to transportation companies which are used for the purposes of immigration will not be renewed this year. Transportation companies will receive no premiums to bring immigrants to Canada to take the place of our own people.
The Old Age Pension Act represents one of the most generous gestures made by this parliament. It is a fine thought when we consider that the old people who are destitute will be helped. I consider it is the duty of the state to give help to those who cannot earn a livelihood because of their advanced years. With this in mind the federal government passed legislation which was accepted by all the provinces from British Columbia to Ontario.
Last year I had occasion to bring before this house the question of low salaries in Quebec. I did so conscientiously to bring the attention of the whole country to the situation as it existed in that province. I mention that fact, Mr. Speaker, because when I referred to the subject last year some hon. members in the far corner of the house said they thought it would be rather inappropriate to discuss the matter, because there was a function in the city of Hull that evening and it was their opinion that the matter should not be before the house. To my mind, the question of low salaries is one of the utmost importance in Canada. I bring it before the house because this is the place where we can more easily broadcast matters of national importance. The situation of the working men in Quebec was very unsatisfactory. A year ago I took the opportunity to speak to the house on that subject, and hon. members were kind enough to listen to my remarks. For the satisfaction of my hon. friends in the far comer of the house may I say that there: has been a change in the province of Quebec. I would not say that the change has resulted from what I said, but I shall tell you of what took place. First of all, there was the genera] report for the year 1929, by the Minister of Public Works and Labour of the province of Quebec. This report, dealing with the minimum wage law for women, was brought down on the 2nd of July, 1929. The speech referred to was delivered on June 12, and two or three weeks later that report was sent to the minister. They had been working on the matter for three years, but almost directly after that little speech they published the report and sent it to the minister.
That is a very small thing, perhaps, but there is more to be said. Last year complaint was made that the Minister of Labour for Quebec had no information as to the wages paid the working men in that province. In 1928 a list of questions was sent to 454 different labour groups, and answers were received from only 245. In 1929, 466 groups were questioned, and answers were received from 280, an increase of 35. That is not much, but it shows good will on the part of these people, and I am surprised that the minister was not sufficiently interested to send his officials to the leaders of the unions in order to get more complete information.
There is something else which brings consolation. A provincial member of the Quebec legislature drafted a minimum wage law for

Unemployment-Mr. Pouliot
men. The matter was discussed by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association; they considered the bill which was introduced in the legislature by Mr. Aime Guertin, member for Hull. During the discussion by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association reference was made to a judgment of the supreme court in regard to a minimum wage law for men in British Columbia, and the association was under the impression that that minimum wage law was declared ultra vires. As a matter of fact it was only an order of the board of adjustment that was declared ultra vires by the Supreme Court of Canada, which said that the board misconceived the nature and scope of its function, and the order which was made was declared ultra vires and invalid. The decision was given in the case of the International Timber Company against Field, judgment being rendered by the Chief Justice. The act itself was not declared ultra vires.
The most extraordinary feature, Mr. Speaker, is that the federated trades council of Quebec declared that a minimum wage enacted by statute would cause great difficulty, and might be taken as the maximum wage by the employers. These people declared themselves opposed to the establishment by statute of a minimum wage for working men. The minimum wage law introduced by Mr. Guertin is referred to in the Montreal Gazette of March 22, where Mr. Guertin is quoted as saying:
This act shall apply to the provincial government as well as to the municipal school corporations.
Then the Gazette goes on to say:
It is on this latter clause that the bill will be found out of order, since it affects the revenues of the jjrovince and, therefore, can only be brought down by a minister with a companion resolution. In drawing up the bill this fact _ is emphasized, because the clause is placed within brackets, as done with government bills accompanied by resolutions. The result will be, therefore, that there may not be even a debate on the principle involved.
As a matter of fact, the minimum wage bill was ruled out of order, and the Ottawa Citizen of March 27 has the following to say:
Because it involved the expenditure of public funds, Speaker Bouchard ruled out of order the bill of Aime Guertin, Conservative, Hull, to the effect that there be established a minimum wage rate for men of 35 cents an hour. The speaker called the attention of Mr. Guertin to the clause which provides that employees of the provincial government come under the act, suggesting a change be made before he made his ruling definite.
Mr. Guertin argued the point, refusing to withdraw the clause. The bill was ruled out of order.

Mr. Guertin has put a motion on the order paper to the effect that "this house invites the government to introduce at the next session an act to fix the minimum salary of certain classes of male workers."
That is quite an improvement. We have not succeeded yet; the question has not been decided, but it is under consideration, and the day will come when the province of Quebec will have by all means a minimum wage law for men. As I stated last year, the maximum wages in Montreal for nine trades are lower than the average wage paid for the same work in twelve important cities from coast to coast.
The other day I was speaking on immigration, and a friend of mine for whom I have much respect said that a remark I made was nonsense. Perhaps that word may be a boomerang. At the time I said there was only one minimum wage law for men, and that was in British Columbia. Another member, who is not here and whose name I will not mention, said there was one in Alberta, and the other hon. gentleman stated there was one in Ontario for men and women as well. I said that if such laws were in effect in Alberta and in Ontario I did not know about it, and I wired the Minister of Labour for Ontario as follows:
Hon. F. E. Godfrey,
Minister of Health and Labour,
Toronto.
Please wire me if there is minimum wage law for men and women in Ontario and, if so, since when is it in force.
That wire was dated March 24, and Mr. Godfrey was good enough to answer me by wire the same day, as follows:
Minimum wage law in Ontario applies to women only. In force now.
Evidently the hon. member who interjected the remark about Ontario forgot that the law applied only to women. I have here a copy of the Ontario act, which is headed, "An act to provide for a minimum wage board with power to regulate in certain cases the minimum wages of women and girls." Can men be considered as being women and girls? I have also the orders of the minimum wage board regarding the employment of women in the province of Ontario, and they will convince my hon. friend that it is dangerous to make preposterous statements.
Apparently some good has come out of the exposure made in the House of Commons as to the terrible state of affairs which exists in the province of Quebec. That province claimed at first that the Old Age Pension Act was ultra vires, tout they seem to have changed

Unemployment-Mr. Church
their minds. The speech from the throne delivered to the Quebec legislature on January 7 last contains this paragraph:
Several social problems of great importance are now up for consideration. Attempts have been made with more or less success to solve some of these in the other provinces and abroad. My ministers do not wish to be behind hand and intend to submit to you a bill appointing a commission composed of economists, to study the various systems of social insurance, of foster homes for children, of old age pensions and several other similar social questions. My ministers think that an exhaustive consideration of these different problems, in the light of experience gained elsewhere, will lead to their satisfactory solution.
I would point out to my hon. friends in the far corner of the house that that province considers this matter to be within its scope. In accordance with that speech fiom the throne a bill has been presented to the provincial house, and the provincial Minister of Labour has said that within three months the commission provided for will come into existence. I hope that that commission will not be used as a smoke screen in an effort to make the people believe that the government is coming to their rescue when in fact it does not intend to do anything. Conditions in Quebec are very bad; my hon. friends know that the day labourer is paid only from $2 to S2.50 per day, while the average is much higher in the other provinces. I do not intend to read the statistics which I gave last year to the house, but is not this matter taken as a whole worthy of due consideration?
Congestion in the big cities is brought about by the influx of people from the country, and one means of preventing unemployment would be to demonstrate to the country people that they would be much better off if they remained on the farms. They would be more independent and happier; during the bad years they would have at least sufficient to live on, and during the good years they would be farther ahead.
I take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. member for North Winnipeg and the hon. member for East Calgary on the manner in which they have discussed this question. It is not a matter to be discussed with heat; it should be considered calmly and with the idea of obtaining results. The hon. member for North Winnipeg said that it was the duty of the government to call a conference of the nine provinces in order that this matter might be studied. That would seem to prove that he himself is inclined to believe that the matter is one which comes within the provincial jurisdiction, because if it did not the government would have no
reason to call a conference. Even if there is no vote upon his motion I believe he has attained his object, because 'he has brought this matter to the attention of the country, as I, in my very humble way, did last year regarding the low wages paid in Quebec. When such matters as these are discussed with moderation there is not a man in the country who is not interested in them and who does not give consideration to the best way of remedying the conditions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter of unemployment is one regarding which every large municipality has made representations to the house during the past three or four months. This government seems to be unlike any other government the world over, because they have simply sat down and fiddled with this question and have made a political football out of it. The first duty of a government is to look after the health, welfare and comfort of its people, but I begin to wonder whether or not we are living in a Christian country when we see this government treating human beings in such a manner. If we should love our neighbours as overselves, then before this parliament closes the government should do something about unemployment. Nine-tenths of the time of the Labour government of Great Britain is taken up in the consideration of the unemployment problem. The United States government, under the administration of Mr. Hoover, has appointed an economic committee composed of the brightest minds in labouring, manufacturing, agricultural, railway and other fields, to meet at Washington in an endeavour to solve the problem of unemployment.
No effort has been made to solve that question in this country. We have a Labour department, but it does not exist so far as unemployment is concerned. Unemployment has never been as bad since confederation as it is at the present time in the large municipalities in this country. Delegations have met the government, but no results have been obtained. The government shelters itself behind technicalities. The house was told a few years ago that unemployment was a matter for the provinces and the municipalities; last session the word "municipality" was struck out, and we were told that it was a matter for the provinces alone-the government refuse to answer the question at all this present session. While I have a high regard for the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) I contend that he has failed utterly to conceive what the government's duty is to
Unemployment-Mr. Church

the unemployed of this country. The government shelters itself behind that celebrated document the British North America Act, which act would appear to be preventing this country from solving any of its economic problems. Unemployment should be the charge of the federal authorities for the reason that they make the tariff; they are in control of the banking laws, the immigration laws and many other items which are set out in section 91 of the British North America Act as being under federal jurisdiction. They say:	We
have had a meeting with the provincial authorities. We seem to have provincial government in the federal sense as regards not only water powers but every other problem. The provinces seem to be running the country because in regard to everything we propose, it seems that we must consult the provinces. This particular question has been made a political football of by the government. The resolution moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) is long overdue in the house. We have been here for five or six weeks and we have not had time in this chamber to take up the most important problem confronting Canada to-day, namely, the unemployment situation as it affects all the provinces of confederation.
The minister relies on the index system. The index system has been weighed in the balance and found wanting. I can show as regards industries in Toronto where this is the case. I know a man who received two weeks' employment in his industry during 1929, and who is listed as having been employed all the year round. According to reports, the British system and the United States system have been weighed in the balance and found wanting. As an index of employment it is far from being accurate. It covers only a few industries; it does not cover the key industries at all. The government send down a form and the industries fill it out. Some of the men may be working only five or six days or a couple of weeks in the year, but they are listed as being employed all the year round. The government say that there is practically no unemployment. All I can find out that the government have been doing during the past five or six years in regard to the unemployment situation is that they have established an unemployment bureau in Ottawa. They have provided an "ambassador" cure for unemployment, and they are sending out over the seven seas ambassadors to different countries, hoping by that method to cure unemployment. That is all the government have done. Since this government have been in power 1,300,000 people have gone to the United States and 
the exodus is still going on. We hear talk about the exodus of raw material. What about the exodus of Canadians who are going to the United States to-day and draining this country of its people? From the last issue of the University of Toronto Monthly I found that of the graduating class in medicine sixty-one stayed in Canada, fifty-seven went to the United States and fifteen to other foreign countries. In other words, 50 to 55 per cent went out of the country. The other day I saw a line-up of 347 men in Toronto on Yonge street near Gerrard, a long line of young men in front of a religious mission, waiting to get a bite to eat at the lunch hour. Anybody passing in the street car could have seen the crowd. In other parts of the country soup kitchens were opened up last winter. The government are asleep at the switch. When you ask them to solve any problem, what do they say? They say: We have nothing to do with it; it is a matter for the provinces, the municipalities.
It is the present tariff policy of the government that has put the workers out on the street, because that is where they are owing to the pan-American tariff of the government. As for their immigration policy, they cannot provide jobs for the men we have in this country now and they are still bringing them in. The first thing we ought to do is to set up an all-Canadian policy and to give jobs for the native-born Canadians, instead of having them to go to the United States to help build up that country. In the cities of Buffalo, Cleveland, Erie, Pennsylvania, Toledo and Detroit we have on the United States border of Lake Erie a cluster of cities that are becoming the largest Canadian cities we have. As Senator Couzens said, Detroit is becoming the third largest Canadian city. This process is going on all the time and immigration is to blame. No other province is suffering more than Ontario from unemployment at the present time. Ontario is losing thousands of its citizens in its cities and towns. The city of Toronto is spending $12,000,000 to $13,000,000 a year in maintaining its children in public and high schools and many of these children who are now ten or twelve years of age will, in the next five or six years, be going over bag and baggage to the United States looking for positions. Ontario has been a dumping ground for1 dairy produce, agricultural produce, coming in from the United States, but the government refuse to do anything; they sit still and say: We have nothing to do with unemployment. The minister says: I will find a permanent cure for it-unemployment insurance. The report of the royal

Unemployment-Mr. Church
commission in the United States shows that it is not a permanent cure for unemployment. It is a policy of robbing Peter to pay Paul, and imposing an additional burden on srtuggling industry. I believe in the principle of unemployment insurance, but in this country we have a state of affairs which is quite different from that of other countries. The policy of the government seems to be that nothing that can be purchased in the United States should be bought in Canada, especially eastern Canada, and that anything that cannot be purchased in the United States should be bought preferably in Europe, the first preference being given to Germany.
The Labour department has fallen down; it might as well close up shop for all the help it has been to the toilers and workers of Canada. The Labour department has failed to fulfil the functions for which it was created, namely to look after labour in the country, create jobs and protect the workers. The Alien Labour Act to-day is a dead letter. A couple of years ago when Sir Henry Drayton, then member for West York, was away, I wrote a letter to the minister. Some nurserymen in Sir Henry Drayton's riding complained that thirty-six workers had been brought in from southern Europe to work in the gardens of West York. I could not get a reply, but I found out afterwards that the minister said in the house that the question of the enforcement of the Alien Labour Act was a matter for the attention of the provincial attorney general. Anything to get out from under! Is it any wonder we have unemployment in Canada?
The other day the Prime Minister said at a dinner that freedom, equality and the end of privilege constituted the policy of twentieth century Liberalism. Yet he says: We have nothing to do with the condition and lot of the people among whom we live; unemployment is a matter for somebody else. Is freedom one of the principles of twentieth century Liberalism? Economic slavery to the United States is what the workers have in place of freedom. That is what the policy of the present government has given instead of freedom. Equality! There is no such thing as equality in this country. The government have a tariff policy of robbing Peter to pay Paul. Talk about the end of privilege in this country 1 Did you ever hear anything like it in your life? They give away the Seven Sisters falls, the Beauharnois water powers and the other water powers of the country. It looks to me as if the government to-day is a government of big interests and appetites instead of a government of freedom, equality and the end of privilege. The
twentieth century Liberals were told the other night by one of them who was making a speech in eulogy of the Prime Minister: Liberalism is the open road. Yes, Liberalism is the open road to the United States. The policy of the government has been responsible for the unemployment existing in this country to-day. Liberalism has been the open road for hundreds of thousands of our working people who have had to leave this country to seek a living in the United States. There has been no concerted effort on the part of this government to deal with this problem in a constructive way.
I have before me the report of the committee on education and labour of the United States congress, presided over by Senator Couzens, of Detroit. The committee was charged with considering the question of unemployment and ascertaining what the causes were. They found that unemployment may be divided under three heads. I would like to give a few examples of what that committee found in that great country to the south where our young men had to go to look for a living.
The committee find, first of all, that there is cyclical unemployment, unemployment that occurs in a cycle, just like children have diphtheria or the measles. That kind of unemployment is with us most of the time, and how to deal with that form of unemployment is the first duty of the government. A wise and up-to-date government will declare active war on unemployment all the time it is in office, because the government of the day is charged with the responsibility of dealing with this problem. The problem must be faced and dealt with in a large and constructive manner that will redound to the benefit of the toilers in this country.
Secondly, there is seasonal unemployment, which comes on us periodically. They are tackling that problem in the United States to-day, and they have a solution for it. I have already referred to the evidence given by Mr. Willard, president of the Baltimore and Ohio Railway before the senate committee. He said:
It is a dangerous thing to have a large number of unemployed men and women-dangerous to society as a whole-dangerous to the individuals who constitute society. When men who are willing and able to work and want to work are unable to obtain work, we need not be surprised if they steal before they starve. Certainly I do not approve of stealing, but if I had to make the choice between stealing and starving, I would surely not choose to starve-and in that respect I do not think I am much unlike the average individual.
The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, as one of the units of society, ought to recognize and carry whatever responsibility rests upon it as
Unemployment-Mr. Church

a large employer, and I think, Mr. Chairman, that it was due to our recognition in part of the obligation which I have just been discussing, that we of the Baltimore and Ohio developed a quickened sense of the importance of anything which had to do with the stabilization of employment. I do not hesitate to say that I should personally feel very much ashamed if it were made clear to me that the Baltimore and Ohio Company was not doing all that it could and ought to do, having due regard for the interests of the owners of the property while other employers of labour were fully meeting similar obligations.
The views which I have just expressed concerning this matter are in large degree held by all employers of labour at the present time. In any event I think there is a more universal appreciation of the obligation resting on employers because of our economic system than ever before, and this has led to what I may refer to as a changed point of view, of a changed state of mind, and it is due to that state of mind, in my opinion, more than to any other single thing that the efforts have been made in recent years, which certainly have been made by employers in all lines of business, to deal with this matter in a more constructive manner.
The third cause of unemployment is technological. It is caused chiefly through the introduction of machines that supplant the worker. Men find that their skill is no longer needed. Let me give you a few examples as found in this report:
Seven men now do the work which formerly required 60 to perform in easting pig iron; 2 men now do the work which formerly required 128 to perform in loading pig iron; one man replaces 42 in operating open-hearth furnaces.
In machine and railway repair shops one man replaces 25 skilled machinists with a gang of 5 or 10 semi-automatic machines; 4 men can now do in 3 to 7 hours what it formerly took 8 men 3 weeks to perform in repair work on locomotives, due to the oxyacetylene torch. Fifteen years ago it took 15 to 30 hours to turn one pair of locomotive tires; now it takes 8 hours to turn 6 pairs with same number of men by use of modern processes.
A brick-making machine in Chicago makes 40,000 bricks per hour. It formerly took one man 8 hours to make 450.
The most up-to-date automatic bottle-making machine makes in one hour what it would take more than 41 workers to make by hand in the manufacture of 4 ounce oval prescription bottles. In 25 and 40 watt electric bulbs the man-hour output of the automatic machine is more than thirty-one times that of the hand process.
In New York from 1914 to 1925 the number of workers in the paper-box industry decreased 32 per cent, while the output per wage earner increased 121 per cent.
Thousands of skilled musicians with a life's training behind them are being thrown out of employment by the advent of the talking movie. In the field of news transportation the Simplex and the Multiplex machines have eliminated the need of trained telegraphers, and to-day by the mere process of typing a message at the sending office, the message is automatically printed at the receiving office. Many thousands of trained telegraphers have been made unneces-

sary during the last few years as a result of this new device. In the printing trades new inventions in typesetting threaten to make possible the setting of type in innumerable offices scattered as many as 500 miles away by the manipulation of keys in a central plant.
That is what they call technological unemployment. It is evident that in the United States they are dealing with this problem of unemployment in a large, constructive way, conducting an active warfare not only on cyclical unemployment, but on seasonal unemployment, and on this newer form, technological unemployment. They are to-day getting results in the United States. The report of this committee has been presented and adopted by congress.
On motion of Mr. Church the debate was adjourned.
